A vast network of galaxies called the Giant Arc has been discovered through the DES Year 1 source catalog, spanning approximately 10 billion light-years. This structure is observed at a significant angle and is seen to extend across the sky over 1.5 degrees. By comparing it to the Sloan Great Wall, the most substantial known structure in the universe at the time, the Giant Arc is found to be nearly four times as large in terms of angular size. It is estimated that this wall consists of about 1,000 galaxies and is viewed as it is, with minimal redshift, which places it around 7-9 billion light-years away. Analysis using the MICE simulation suggests that the Giant Arc likely represents a massive and extensive structure that spans around 480 million light-years when viewed from its source, and it is observed as it is, with minimal redshift, which places it around 4.4-5.2 billion light-years away. It is worth noting that this finding requires verification due to the methods used, and it is the first time a massive wall-like structure has been identified through X-ray data.

Wide-field photometry encompasses techniques that allow for the measurement of sky brightness across a broad area. By utilizing wide-field photometry without absolute calibration, researchers can determine the vertical aerosol optical depth. The method relies on comparing observed values of the standard luminosity function to a simulated set of values, both under similar conditions of optical depth and color. Theoretical simulations demonstrate the potential for achieving a precision of 0.02 in vertical aerosol measurements. In practice, the method may be implemented using existing wide-field photometry surveys such as Pan-STARRS or LSST. The approach also offers a way to calibrate absolute magnitudes of celestial sources based on relative measurements. In the case of extragalactic objects, this could provide a more precise method of determining the distances to high-luminosity objects like supernovae than traditional techniques.

We tackle the challenge of recovering the pose of objects within a scene that contains various types of occlusions and overlapping objects. Our primary contribution involves expanding the proven projection grouping principle to employ curvature-based object descriptions. By analyzing projected shadow shapes, our system identifies potential poses for embedded objects and weighs their likelihood through a metric that measures the distance between two objects in 3D space. Our approach prioritizes objects with more distinct shapes as priority targets, resulting in a focus on estimating the pose of key objects even in complex scenes. Our experiments demonstrate that our curvature-based approach produces accurate pose estimates and outperforms traditional features in scenarios with partial or hidden information. Additionally, our system shows its ability to adapt to various scenes and excel in projection grouping without prior knowledge of the scene's contents.

A peridynamic model that incorporates a bond-based kernel with a micro-mechanical interpretation is presented for a time-dependent, nonlinear elasticity framework. This model is applied to a non-degenerate sectorial kernel, leading to the solution of a history-dependent elasticity problem on a finite time interval with initial conditions. The solution is demonstrated to belong to a space of continuous functions, and this result is coupled with an existence proof for a stationary problem. Furthermore, the model is modified to account for the growth of cracks over time, and the solution is found to be part of a space characterized by unbounded lower dimensions. This research lays the groundwork for studying a variety of non-standard elasticity models.

This research builds upon the Graphical Lasso framework by introducing a new method, 
Fancy Lasso, that incorporates latent variables to enhance the model. By dividing the
precision matrix into two parts, with one representing the latent variables' 
covariances and the other the observable variables' connections, we minimize the 
rank of the matrix to achieve sparsity. We demonstrate that this method surpasses 
the performance of Graphical Lasso in a simulation study and facilitate the 
efficient computation of Fancy Lasso via an active set algorithm. Additionally, 
we apply and successfully evaluate our method on two real-world datasets, the 
MMID gene expression dataset and the NCI connectome dataset.

To assess the performance of classical force fields for alanine dipeptide in an explicit aqueous environment, accurate reference data are necessary. These references can be obtained through the simultaneous solution of the Schr\"{o}dinger and Nambu equations, which describes the coupled evolution of a quantum system and its surrounding classical environment. Numerical solutions to the integrated equations of motion vary significantly depending on the method, potentially influencing computations. In this study, we evaluate and compare the efficiency and accuracy of four distinct numerical approaches: the time-dependent variational Hamiltonian method with a semi-classical Hamiltonian, the multi-configurational time-dependent self-consistent field technique with a Hamiltonian defined by the minimum drift approximation, the time-dependent renormalized independent-particle model, and the adiabatic state initialization method, with and without the renormalization of nonadiabatic verieties. Our test system consists of an alanine dipeptide molecule, treated either quantum mechanically or through time-dependent renormalization, surrounded by 222 water molecules. To evaluate the methods, we analyze their performance in achieving accurate reference energies for various states of the system across different levels of system complexity, utilizing both short and extended integration periods. Our results indicate that while the time-dependent renormalized independent-particle model yields the most accurate energies, other methods such as the minimum drift approximation, for instance, offer a good compromise between efficiency and accuracy, especially in longer simulations exceeding 1 picosecond.

Using numerical simulations, we investigated the long-term behaviors of binary black holes in an surrounding matter field, specifically in an ergodic disk. The simulation included various parameters such as binary separation, initial eccentricity, and disk temperature, which affects the behavior of gravitational waves. The influence of the disk was examined under both high and low temperature conditions. The findings show that in a hot disk, the binary starts emitting waves in the high-frequency range and then moves to the low-frequency range, eventually leading to merger. In contrast, a cold disk leads to more rapid, eccentric orbits. Additionally, a cold disk causes increased emission of gravitational waves during the initial stages due to the greater interaction with the binary. The influence of the disk also extends to direct collisions with the binary, particularly in a cold disk, where the likelihood of such events is increased. The influence of the disk extends to direct collisions with the binary, particularly in a cold disk, where the likelihood of such events is heightened. The simulation demonstrates the importance of pre-detector systems in potential space-based gravitational wave observatories, as even binaries at millions of lightyears may influence observations due to their significant signal-to-noise ratio.

We investigate a theoretical model comprising a star-shaped graph, where a stiff central edge is connected to three flexible edges with limited elasticity at their junctions. The exponential stability of this symmetric vibrational state is proven for temperatures that fall within a broad range. Additionally, our analysis reveals that internal energy releases exponential instability on the slopes of the edges within specific frequency bands. In contrast, the exponential stability of the given symmetric state can be achieved through external periodic driving if the frequencies of the edge and the driver align, such as in cases where the edge and the driver have the same frequency in a particular multiple relationship.

This research is focused on gathering essential data about the acoustic properties of a specialized adhesive, known as Stycast 1090SI, as it is widely used in various high-impedance material applications and there is a notable lack of information available on its sound-conducting characteristics. To collect this information, the adhesive was compared to PMMA (polymethyl methacylate) by measuring its acoustic impedance and attenuation through multiple methods, including ultrasonic measurement and by analyzing the transmitted sound waves. Two different configurations of sample layers were tested: single layers with varying thicknesses and layered combinations of PMMA and Stycast 1090SI. The findings revealed that Stycast 1090SI possesses similar acoustic properties to PMMA, with an almost identical acoustic impedance and relatively minor differences in attenuation. These findings are consistent across all measurement techniques, demonstrating an effective reduction of sound wave reflection at the interface between PMMA and Stycast 1090SI, which facilitates seamless sound transmission and accurate ultrasonic measurements through layers of this adhesive.

In complex multilayer networks, assigning values to nodes or other elements is referred to as labeling. The North-Western European Power Grid is an example of such a network, consisting of multiple interconnected transmission layers with distinct voltage levels. To efficiently operate this grid, optimal peer-to-peer trading strategies between nodes are needed. However, these strategies depend on inter-layer constraints affecting the importance of nodes within each layer. Previously, a variant of the multilayer Schriber method was used to determine the importance of these nodes, but this method disregards the effects of an external field on the importance of corresponding nodes across different layers. In response, a new attraction-based approach has been developed to compute the importance of nodes in multilayer networks under the influence of an external field. This approach is then applied to the North-Western European Power Grid, demonstrating a significant difference in the calculated node importance when compared to traditional methods. Additionally, this study highlights the impact of an external field on the operation of trading strategies in this grid, enabling more effective peer-to-peer trading.

A comprehensive investigation into the color-dependent point-spread function's influence on imaging quality was conducted. This research examined how the color-dependent point-spread function impacts images taken with a camera, applying both empirical and theoretical analyses. Different methods were used to calculate the color-dependent point-spread function, and their results were compared and contrasted. Various metrics were also applied to assess the color-dependent point-spread function's effect on image clarity, demonstrating its impact across various modulation functions and apertures. Additionally, the relationship between the color-dependent point-spread function and spatial frequency was explored, revealing how the color-dependent point-spread function affects the clarity of images across different frequencies.

A recent study on the Dirac equation in $R$-Minkowski spacetime has been conducted, yielding a modified equation that mimics its counterpart in de Sitter spacetime, with the additional benefit of being compatible with the gauge $R=0$. The investigation into $R$-Minkowski spacetime may provide valuable insights into understanding spacetime's inherent curvature and its potential implications for particle physics beyond the standard model.

The 'cdt' package introduces an implementation of causal graph modeling in R, comprising key elements like structural equation models, causal chains, and mediating variables, ultimately aiming to estimate direct and total causal effects via the R 'estim' package.

This study employs high-speed imaging and pressure measurements to investigate the surface seal of a rotating cavity with an impact-generated vortex, focusing on the effects of increasing speed and pressure reduction inside the cavity. The surface of the rotating cavity was made non-leakage by a flat surface, and the results showed that, at moderate speeds, the surface movement was consistent with an imaginary circle, but as the speed increased, the movement became irregular and the pressure reduction inside the cavity intensified. As the speed increased, the size of the vortex core decreased, but the movement of the surface continued to be affected until the highest speed tested, indicating that the impact of a large size of nine-dots (approximately five times the core) remains significant. However, the pressure reduction inside the cavity had a more pronounced effect, and the results indicated a clear shift from the influence of the vortex to the impact of the vortex core at the highest speed tested, highlighting the complexity of this phenomenon.

Following the generalized Witten effect, we've discovered a connection between the Witten effect and the Dirac delta distribution in the context of charged states in quantum gravity. This has led to an in-depth analysis of the Witten effect's implications, revealing that the cosmological constant must be a multiple of the Witten charge. This charged state is equivalent to the expectation value of the Witten operator, which is linked to the energy-momentum tensor. A key finding shows that the Witten effect can be understood through the intersection of charged cycles in the geometry of AdS$_2$, leading to an extension of the Witten effect to higher dimensions. This involves the introduction of a Witten operator for each non-trivial cycle within the geometry, with each operator representing a distinct multiple of the cosmological constant. These operators are then used to derive the expectation values of the Witten operators, which are expressed as differential forms that capture the behavior of scalar fields on the geometry of AdS$_2$. The global properties of these forms have a clear physical interpretation, which includes the liberation of both left and right zero-modes of the Witten operator, along with the creation of a quasiparticle resembling the Witten operator from the vacuum. The interplay between the geometry of AdS$_2$ and its non-trivial cycles is also shown to result in the generation of an infinite series of the cosmological constant's multiples as charged states in the Witten operator.

Once a mobile application is developed, its underlying framework and built-in tools should provide robust security, free from vulnerabilities that could enable malicious data access. OctopOS is a cutting-edge, adaptable OS framework for Android and iOS devices, designed to prevent malicious data access. It achieves this goal by integrating a state-of-the-art mandatory access control (MAC) system with each application, dividing its memory space into six isolated segments and assigning different access permissions for data within each segment. When the system initializes, it uses a sophisticated binary instrumentation technique to examine the application's underlying code and determine the access permissions based on the program's type and potential security risks. And, unlike other OS frameworks with limited adaptability, OctopOS can easily accommodate changing system conditions and prioritize security over performance considerations. We showcase the capabilities of OctopOS by implementing a diverse set of applications, revealing how its features prevent malicious data access. And in our tests, we find that OctopOS surpasses existing Android and iOS security measures in several areas.

We investigate a critical challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) where an intelligent adversary intentionally hinders the agent's progress by creating undesirable transition dynamics. The existing RL theory typically assumes that the environment makes coherent responses to the agent's actions, but this adversary can force the agent to expend rewards on unnecessary actions, thwarting its progress. To tackle this problem, we develop a sophisticated algorithm called Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG), which ensures the learning guarantee under these corrupted episodes. The FPG algorithm employs a unique clean-experience reward estimation technique to isolate the clean data and accurately evaluate the experience. By leveraging a variety of technical innovations, including an innovative application of the bounded difference condition with a finite action space, we can provide a rigorous performance guarantee for the FPG algorithm, demonstrating that it can achieve a similar regret bound comparable to that in an undisturbed environment, with an additional term proportional to the number of corrupted episodes. Additionally, our results include a specific consequence, namely that uniform filtering can yield an improved regret of O(\sqrt{d}H \log H), which is a significant improvement over the existing upper bound without adversarial interference.

The classic box game paradox has been resolved by determining the optimal strategy, which involves a crucial element: the element of choice. However, this solution does not account for players who make irrational decisions. We introduce a new strategy that takes into consideration the probability of the player selecting any specific element, assuming the player lacks perfect knowledge. This approach leads to a revised understanding of the element of choice and requires the application of advanced mathematical techniques. Specifically, we employ calculus and probability theory to analyze the player's likely action, leading to a more complex solution that involves derivative calculations. The resulting strategy demonstrates that the element of choice is indeed crucial but also subject to variation based on the dispersal of the initial wealth along the number line.

We employ ab initio calculations to examine the properties of cubanite, a significant compound found in uranium ores, which has drawn interest due to its remarkable resistance to both chemical and structural changes and its unusual magnetic behavior. Using the PBE+U method and incorporating structural and antiferromagnetic considerations, we identify the stable charge distribution in cubanite as evenly distributed across all 5f orbitals of uranium, which also explains its ability to maintain stability under varying charges and resist structural changes. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the electronic structure of the U$^{4+}$ ions in cubanite promotes the alignment of all uranium spins in the same direction, resulting in a robust ferromagnetic ordering. Moreover, our study shows that the strong coordination of uranium to its neighboring oxygen and copper atoms hinders the transfer of electrons and prevents cubanite from becoming a conductor, which we have verified through experimental means. Overall, our theoretical analysis provides a comprehensive understanding of the unique properties in cubanite.

We investigate a quantum dot coupled to an acoustic cavity using laser pulses to induce Rabi oscillations between the dot and cavity states. The driving laser has a specific frequency and polarization, which can be adjusted to optimize the outcome. Our findings show that fine-tuning the driving laser's frequency to match the energy difference between the dot and a higher energy state in the cavity can significantly impact Rabi oscillations, potentially trapping the system in a particular state. This effect is influential even when the cavity is not initially occupied, and it may have implications for using acoustic cavities as sensitive detectors.

We examine a one-dimensional herringbone lattice where two kinds of atoms, with different masses and interaction strengths, are arranged in an alternating pattern. Our analysis begins with an unperturbed Hamiltonian, but we then introduce a variation that phasing-matches the interactions between adjacent sites, effectively creating a two-dimensional equivalent of the lattice. Our main focus is on investigating the lattice's phonon dynamics via the dispersion relation of its excitations, and we identify multiple regions of interest based on the interatomic interaction's incommensurability. Our study demonstrates that varying the lattice's prototypical structure through this perturbation results in the phonons' monodromy caps shifting in response, resulting in the formation of unusual features within the Brillouin zone. Additionally, our findings showcase how this perturbation allows for the lattice's symmetry to be broken by means of irreducible representations, ultimately yielding a state where the lattice's monodromy group undergoes a singular transformation.

We examine single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) generated via beam splitters and parametric amplifiers, comparing their properties and likelihood of occurrence. By analyzing two scenarios, one involving a beam splitter with two input coherent states and another with a parametric amplifier driven by a single coherent state, we find significant differences in success probabilities for both cases. Our findings indicate that beam splitter-based SPCCSs possess a higher probability of achieving the desired state of action, with a value of $10^{-4}$, as opposed to the amplifier-based SPCCSs which have a much lower chance of $10^{-8}$. Our study suggests that employing beam splitters over parametric amplifiers could significantly enhance the likelihood of creating SPCCSs in optical systems.

The paper presents a novel algebraic decomposition of complex coefficients in the Newman-Penrose formalism, simplifying their relationship to a straightforward differential equation based 4-component potential representation. This innovative expression offers a clear understanding of the complex coefficients in terms of physical electromagnetic wave characteristics, specifically elliptical, circular, and linear polarization, alongside a formula for calculating the polarization state. The resulting expression offers an intuitive visual representation of the Weyl scalar quantities through a complex plane plot, effectively illustrating the polarization of gravitational waves generated by various massive objects in astrophysical environments.

Researchers utilize knowledge graphs to represent complex polymers using a novel approach that rethinks their depiction. This method views a polymer as a local structure, made up of specific monomers, rather than an ordered sequence of monomers along the polymer chain. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, a suite of tasks including monomer prediction, link prediction, and categorical property prediction are performed on a dataset derived from the BiPolimer database. These experiments show that the proposed approach achieves impressive results, outperforming existing sequential models in all tasks. For instance, it accurately predicts 76.5% of monomers within a local structure and 71.9% of categorical property targets. Furthermore, it demonstrates a high degree of transparency, with 73.2% of inferred monomers also present in the training set. To further understand its capabilities, a case study is conducted on a dataset containing cancer-associated mutations in polymer structures, revealing that the model can effectively identify mutational hotspots. The source code for these experiments is available openly.

During a pandemic, the rapid spread of a new contagious disease may lead to healthcare systems being overwhelmed, causing shortages in vital equipment such as ventilators. To mitigate this shortage, we propose a method called asynchronous ventilation, which allows a single ventilator to be shared among multiple patients by briefly disconnecting the ventilator from one patient and reconnecting it to another. We develop a control algorithm for this process and ensure that each patient receives their desired tidal volume. We also examine the dynamics of the system in detail and provide a safety margin to prevent over-inflation of lungs. We implemented our method on a realistic simulation and successfully demonstrated its effectiveness.

Recently, attention-based models have gained popularity due to their success in various medical image segmentation tasks. To adapt this successful approach for use with limited training data, the Dilated Dense Attention Unet was introduced. In this research, we modify the network by incorporating a Dense Attention Module and dilated convolutional layers to enhance model performance while reducing parameter counts. Our method is applied to esophageal tumor segmentation with limited annotated scans, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness.

The process of evaluating formations in real-time involves complex computations, necessitating a balanced trade-off between performance and memory utilization to optimize speed without exceeding available memory limits. To address this challenge, a novel approach called LM-EnRML was developed, leveraging the benefits of an energy-efficient convolutional neural network (CNN) while adapting existing memory optimization techniques to optimize both energy consumption and memory utilization. In contrast to prior solutions, this method combines deep learning models with linear transformations to enhance speed and accuracy without resorting to explicit layer unrolling. Instead, LM-EnRML employs automatic differentiation to efficiently minimize loss functions, directly utilizing memory-efficient deep learning models. When applied to a synthetic data set, LM-EnRML significantly boosts performance, achieving a 5-fold increase in speed with comparable accuracy. Additionally, LM-EnRML exhibits superior performance in actual field data evaluations, outperforming existing methods by 3-5 times in terms of speed.

This paper offers a new perspective on how the inclusion of corpus-level information affects NLP models. Rather than focusing on explanations for human-generated ratings or predictions, the authors are concerned with understanding the impact of corpus-level information on automated NLP tasks. To investigate this, they developed a suite of tasks that rely on the automatic extraction of entities, relations, and classification from text. The results of these experiments revealed significant gains, with improvements ranging from 8% to 15% in F1 score, when using a pre-trained model without fine-tuning. This led the authors to consider various mechanisms for incorporating corpus-level information and found that pre-trained models already contain useful entity-level information that is released during training. This finding challenged the authors' initial hypothesis that the inclusion of corpus-level information would lead to overfitting and highlighted the potential of tapping into pre-trained models' entity-level knowledge for other NLP applications.

We analyze how the tropical pre-image of a rational 2-dimensional quartic curve, considered in a universal cover of complex space, relates to its complex counterpart. We demonstrate that this connection enables determination of the geometry of twisted edges within the tropicalized curve. A corresponding study on tropical K3 surfaces concludes that certain four-gons within a proper tropicalization of a rational complex quartic surface do not correspond to the starting points of any bitangents in that surface. Furthermore, this result is applied to a specific family of tropical K3 surfaces to show that their corresponding complex counterparts have an irrational bitangent property.

The objective of this study is to investigate a novel localization approach for mobile robots, based on spatiotemporal point processes, and evaluate its performance in real-world scenarios. This method models surrounding robots as nearby point processes and estimates the time differences between the arrival of adjacent robots to determine the robot's location. Ideal simulation results indicate that this approach can accurately localize robots within 0.4 meters. Real-world implementations, utilizing the Miro platform and with 20 seconds of data, demonstrate an average localization error of 0.61 meters. In contrast to ideal simulations, this method exhibits a higher error due to the presence of outliers caused by delayed or missed packet detections. To mitigate this, the implementation of a threshold for time differences is shown to significantly reduce errors to 0.44 meters.

Despite having over half of the world's population speaking a native language other than English, NLP research has traditionally been predominantly English-centered. This limitation hinders the development of essential language technologies for multilingual communities, which are crucial for cultural preservation, access to information, healthcare, education, and the global economy. To bridge this gap, this survey presents a comprehensive overview of NLP research beyond English, covering topics such as multilingual models, task-based evaluations, NLP applications, and resources. It also explores promising future directions fueled by the integration of NLP and machine learning and highlights the significance of data standardization, which is critical for advancing this research.

The generation of image descriptions is a task that has been effectively automated using machine learning, but in comparison to other applications, its underlying guidelines are somewhat primitive. This relative lack of development limits the potential for a significant user group, namely those who are visually impaired, to benefit from image description capabilities. In our research, a set of rules known as the CAPTIONS guidelines has been created with the goal of guiding machine learning models in producing more accurate and helpful image descriptions, suitable for a broad audience including visually impaired people. To validate the effectiveness of these guidelines, we designed and executed a comprehensive evaluation study in which various models were trained and tested using multiple datasets. Our results indicate that our guidelines can significantly enhance the performance of machine learning models in producing image descriptions that are both visually accurate and linguistically sound. In particular, our research demonstrates the importance of optimizing model performance using a diverse range of evaluation metrics, as this is critical to ensuring that image descriptions are accessible to visually impaired users.

To accurately model the electron energy loss function in tantalum oxide, we've developed a method that accounts for local field effects and spin-orbit coupling, using the HGH percolation method to determine the effective dielectric function. Our approach shows good agreement with more complex simulations and highlights the significance of considering local field effects, spin-orbit coupling, and the HGH percolation method in calculating the electron energy loss function, particularly for semi-conducting and insulating materials with intricate band structures.

A notable phenomenon known as 'The Big Sort' has been observed in the United States, where communities are becoming increasingly geographically isolated. This trend is notable for a dramatic shift in voting patterns, with voters within each community developing greater homogeneity in their voting choices. This research investigates the impact of 'The Big Sort' on the widespread online dissemination of false information among users in culturally divided areas. Our analysis indicates that the phenomena of repeatable behavior and homophily, where users share information to confirm cultural affiliations, can result in false information being spread more efficiently in culturally homogeneous communities. Furthermore, our model shows that cultural homogeneity can lead to the irreversible dominance of false information over time. This research highlights the unintended consequences of repeatable behavior and homophily in culturally divided societies, where false information can spread infinitely due to cultural backing, causing irreparable harm.

Human intelligence can be an incredibly effective force when deployed rapidly and widely, but traditional machine learning often requires significant computational resources or large annotation datasets to train models. We've developed novel, efficient techniques that allow advanced models to achieve exceptional performance on complex tasks while being lightweight and low-cost to train. Utilizing these methods, we've created an impressive array of machine learning models that excel across diverse categories, including classification, perception, retrieval, and generative tasks, even in scenarios with limited labeled data. Our models have not only surpassed human performance in various tasks but have also achieved remarkable success in challenging fields like medical imaging analysis and natural language processing, gaining attention from top research institutions and organizations. Our goal is to empower users without extensive computational expertise to build high-performing machine learning models for their own specific applications.

To gain deeper insights into the dynamics of teaching, our research introduces a novel approach using conversational AI to study how instructions and actions are learned from demonstrations. We develop a framework that allows natural interactions between students and teachers through speech and physical actions, with the aim of observing and analyzing learning processes. By conducting experiments with this framework, our findings reveal the varied semantic concepts expressed during teaching and reveal how different factors like demonstration style, audio instructions, subtasks, and errors significantly impact the speech patterns used. Furthermore, our results show that traditional machine learning methods and neural networks differ in their performance in predicting future speech actions, with the former being more effective in certain situations. Our study demonstrates the capability of our framework to detect notable events, identify conceptual knowledge, and forecast future actions, ultimately demonstrating its potential to explore complex learning processes.

Leags III features an innovative algorithm to generate ordered trees with designated ports, addressing the common issue of most generation methods, which often disregard the outdegrees of specified leaves. To overcome this limitation, the proposed algorithm uses a priority-based ordering system to capture the outdegrees as constraints, thereby enabling the efficient generation of ordered trees that precisely match the input parameters. This approach not only solves the port-equipped generation problem but also provides a general solution for generating trees within specified degree constraints. As a result, the algorithm surpasses the performance of existing methods, achieving a significant speedup of up to 125 times, and has the added benefit of naturally supporting parallelization.

A key challenge in quantum field theory lies in determining the optimal configuration of a nonlinear integral equation, known as the Faddeev equation, which represents the interaction between an N-body system and a linearized quantum field. Building upon previous work, a new set of Euler-Arnold equations has been derived through a simplified variational approach for both internal and relative motion scenarios. Specifically, the paper provides a detailed derivation of the Euler-Arnold equations for N-body problems in motion relative to one body and offers a simplified variational formulation for the equations of motion in the N-body case when motion is confined to a plane.

The rise of conversational interfaces like voice assistants highlights the
need for automated testing frameworks that can precisely mimic user interactions
and assess the systems' performance and reliability. While existing testing tools
focus on functional validation, there is a lack of standardized approaches to
detect defects in conversational applications. Furthermore, developing, executing,
and iterating upon automated tests is hindered by the absence of efficient ways
to simulate user behavior and pinpoint test failures. To address these challenges,
we present ConqaEngine, a testing framework for conversational applications
utilizing Z3, a satisfiability modulo theories solver. This framework
automatically generates test data for user input fields and identifies areas for
improvement by solving satisfiability problems in array and string theories.
Additionally, ConqaEngine incorporates best practices for coding and
execution efficiency, ensuring fast iteration times for developers. To demonstrate
its effectiveness, we applied ConqaEngine to two popular conversational
applications – Dialogflow and AWS Lex – and observed substantial reductions in
development, execution, and iteration times.

We've discovered evidence of an unseen mass with the strength of a full Earth's gravity, present in nearly 90% of the visible sky at a distance of about 300 million light years. This discovery was made possible by examining variations in the gravitational field experienced by a group of 21 Millisecond Pulsars. The effect we're observing is likely the result of moving from one region of mass distribution to another, similar to how tides change as one moves across the Earth. The distribution of this unseen mass is similar to that of the cosmic structure that is observable, and appears to be connected to vast networks of galaxies. It's worth noting that previous research predicted the existence of such structures based on the observable patterns. The phenomenon we're observing could be the movement of matter through the vast networks of galaxies, and it's also possible that it's the result of pulsars moving through a more localized field of mass.

Recently, pre-trained models have significantly boosted machine translation performance. In addition to improving primary translation objectives, other tasks like translation memory retrieval have benefited from these improvements. This task involves selecting the most suitable previous translation from a given set of options based on similarity. The proposed approach introduces a cross-lingual memory retriever model that directly expends on the multilingual capabilities of existing wide-range BERT models, using both similarity matching and contrastive learning techniques. This method is found to enhance translation performance compared to traditional bilingual translation memory approaches, particularly in scenarios with limited data. Experimental results show the proposed approach achieves 11% better performance than the baseline in a low-data setting and 5% in a mid-data setting, ultimately demonstrating the effectiveness of cross-lingual memory retriever models in this task.

Recent research suggests that the unusual characteristics in the cosmic microwave background could be indicative of a specific pattern resulting from the radiation of primordial black holes, specifically those with a mass around the Planck scale. This theory posits that the Hawking radiation of these primordial black holes would result in areas of the microwave background with distinct properties, such as unique variance patterns and localized temperature fluctuations. A new analysis confirms the presence of 'Hawking points' and 'low-variant circles' in the microwave background data, consistent with the predicted characteristics of primordial black hole radiation. However, the findings also reveal that the assumed variances of these patterns need to be adjusted downward by a significant amount, which presents a challenge to the theory. Consequently, any model seeking to verify this theory through the microwave background data must also explain the observed anomalies, such as the axis of evil, the quadrupole anomaly, and the lack of power in the microwave background at certain scales. A new statistical analysis provides a framework for evaluating the credibility of this theory based on the microwave background data and suggests that any model attempting to verify it must possess an excess likelihood of at least 10 times to be considered plausible.

This work builds upon previous research by R. V. Chelsea and Y. Wang, who found solutions to the Yamabe flow in a compact, minimally parabolic manifold with non-negative Ricci curvature and a certain condition on its scalar curvature. The study demonstrated that when this condition is relaxed, the equation has solutions in a compact, minimally parabolic manifold with negative Ricci curvature in certain areas and changing sign, given a certain lower bound on its scalar curvature. The new research establishes that the equation also has solutions in a compact, minimally parabolic manifold with negative Ricci curvature in certain areas and changing sign, given a certain lower bound on its scalar curvature, and a small volume in a certain area. The study also demonstrates that when the manifold's dimension is greater than two, the equation's solution is not linear. The solution was found through a variational approach, utilizing the compactness theorem and the monotonicity formula, and involves a new estimate that may be useful in other applications.

To enhance robustness in few-shot learning, our proposed method, Sample-wise Learning with Memory, integrates a past-experience-based embedding adjustment technique that updates embeddings in a way that previous, related data is taken into consideration. Instead of solely utilizing support samples to create a prototype, SWML utilizes prototype distances from past encounters to define an optimal prototype point. By doing so, SWML successfully mitigates the negative effects of outlier samples within few-shot scenarios. Through extensive experiments on prominent datasets for the tasks of image classification and text classification, our approach demonstrates superior performance, particularly in scenarios with outlier samples, outperforming comparative methods by a margin of at least 5% in accuracy.

This paper delves into the complexities of user preference learning within recommendation systems, examining the challenges posed by limited data and category-based preferences. To address these issues, we introduce the Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module, which facilitates both sparse data remediation and multi-aspect preference capture through focused self-supervised learning. In comparisons to conventional self-supervised learning techniques and comprehensive baseline methods, our proposed framework exhibits remarkable efficacy on diverse datasets, indicating a notable enhancement of up to 125% in recommendation accuracy. Moreover, we provide comprehensive experiments and theoretical insights to demonstrate the benefits of GAPE, showcasing its capacity for addressing the fundamental issues of user preference learning. Our code and data are available for public access, paving the way for further research in this domain.

Exotic cones, which include a wide range of well-known formulations such as copulas, minimal flows, and bicriteria linear programs, have a unified framework through their definition as the intersection of multiple cones. This research examines the relationship between these exotic cones and standard cones, particularly the latter's extensions, in the context of formulations. It's shown that by leveraging this relationship, formulations can be expressed as the intersection of multiple standard cones, potentially leading to a more compact and simpler formulation. This new perspective enables a comparison of these exotic formulations to standard extended formulations, revealing their dimensionality and complexity in a more nuanced light. As evidence, several exotic formulations are reanalyzed and found to possess significantly reduced sizes in comparison to their counterparts. This research may inspire the development of more efficient algorithms, as complex formulations can sometimes be tractable, and this understanding can help identify the feasibility of solving them computationally.

The primary goal of our investigation is to examine the impact of varying training datasets with different image quality on the performance of medical image restoration models. Our ultimate objective is to clarify the optimal approach to creating training datasets that yield superior model results. Specifically, we focus on improving the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of magnetic resonance images, as measured by the structural similarity index (SSIM) and SNR, when using an internal validation set. Our findings show that models trained with images of poorer quality, followed by those with medium and high quality, result in the best outcomes. This pattern holds true across different types of MR images, obtained from different brain regions. It's interesting to note that our results don't consistently support the conventional assumption that models trained with higher quality images inevitably perform better. These findings contribute valuable insights to the complex field of medical image processing, offering a more nuanced understanding of the relationships between image quality, data composition, and model performance.

This research introduces a network-based framework for a type of multi-agent optimization problem known as consensus optimization or multi-agent optimization. Within this framework, individual agents represent sub-problems that contribute to an overall optimization goal, and the study demonstrates their connection to the general NLOSP formulation. The framework then applies this understanding to analyze specific cases of network-based multi-agent optimization problems, including resource allocation in wireless networks, optimal power control, and target location in a network, and presents a comprehensive survey of network-based multi-agent optimization problems. Finally, the study highlights the significance of network-based multi-agent optimization in various fields and highlights the potential of relaxed integral solutions to solve complex optimization problems efficiently.

We introduce a file system called `relaxfs` for the NOVA-relaxed NVM memory model, where applications access persistent memory as individual files. Our evaluation shows that, relative to the original NOVA approach, `relaxfs` reduces the overhead of small, persistent writes by a factor of 10-30 and improves file system performance by 1.4-3.7 times. Additionally, `relaxfs` supports both DRAM and solid-state drives (SSDs) as persistent memory technologies, with notable benefits when using Optane DC Persistent Memory Modules (PMMs) for small writes. Our results indicate that file systems like `relaxfs` are essential for maximizing the benefits of current generation PMMs, particularly in workloads with small, persistent data sizes.

The Motivation Dynamics theory was originally designed for individual decision-making analysis and was now adapted for multiple agents in this study. This adaptation introduced a significant innovation to the network optimization field by incorporating a learning rule that reflects each agent's emotional response to satisfaction or discontent. Unlike existing multi-agent models, Motivation Dynamics models do not assume agents have explicit communication or observe the actions of others. Instead, the model relies on a cooperative aspect of the learning process, known as the "dynamics of cooperation". This led the authors to develop an equilibrium analysis, utilizing the concept of a quasi-perfect equilibrium, which provided a clearer understanding of behaviors that emerge through learning, such as the tendency for agents to converge on a common action, such as reaching a mutual understanding on a rendezvous point. To further explore the complexities of Motivation Dynamics, the authors applied the method of successive sections to analyze the learning process for a system in which agents learn simultaneously. This led to the identification of a quasi-perfect equilibrium in the simplified case of two agents with different preferences. Moreover, the authors discussed the implications of their findings for the broader theory of dynamic systems and the learning process.

The study examines the structural and magnetic characteristics of Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds, focusing on Cm content between 0.25 and 0.75. Investigating these alloys with x=0.5, 0.6, and 0.8 allows researchers to explore the effects of Cm concentration on structural, thermal-interval, and local-magnetic-properties by combining X-ray diffraction, dilatometry, specific-heat measurements, and muon-spin relaxation/rotation. Findings reveal that Cm substitution for Gd enhances the unit cell volume, results in a thermal-expansion anomaly around the Cm impurity local moments' freezing temperatures, and exhibits distinct specific-heat features indicative of localized magnetic scattering. Additionally, the predicted 2$\updelta$k$_{B}$T value for Cm moments matches the measured values, confirming the expected moment values and highlighting the significance of interplay between Gd and Cm moments in these alloys. Moreover, the results show that the predicted moment values for Cm hold across all investigated concentrations, with no compensation effect observed in the measured moment values.

By utilizing lattice QCD, a study on the interaction between heavy quarks within different flavor combinations has been conducted. The investigation focused on the motion of heavy quarks while their movement is not completely unconnected, mapping out the dynamics of heavy-quark systems in a complex, multi-flavor setting. The findings show consistent results with heavy-quark rules applying at a somewhat intermediate distance of about one quark radius, and the heavy-quark symmetry holding strong at very close distances. The research has also the opportunity to enhance our comprehension of the interaction between heavy and light quarks within mesons.

For the finite classical Coxeter group Bn, we develop a refined version of the generalized standard OGS, describing its exchange laws in relation to its Coxeter length and descent set. Additionally, we establish a direct connection between our refined version and the standard OGS, specifically its law, and demonstrate how this connection implies the law for Bn is derived from the refined laws of B(n) by fixing the Coxeter length at n.

Theoretical models suggest that cosmic events like Fast Radio Bursts and Gamma-Ray bursts originate from the halos of distant galaxies. To understand these phenomena, researchers need to understand the structure and composition of galactic halos. A recent study analyzed the magnetic fields in the halos of 32 distant galaxies using the Very Large Array and the Very Large Telescope. The findings reveal a consistent pattern where the magnetic fields transition from being aligned with the galaxy's orientation to being perpendicular to it, exhibiting a symmetrical, disk-like structure. This discovery contradicts previous findings showing the magnetic fields are perpendicular to the galaxy's orientation and suggests they may be influenced by the galaxy's orientation. This research also shows that the magnetic fields within the inner regions of the galaxies are more intense than previously measured. The findings provide a clearer picture of the magnetic field structure within galactic halos and the transition within the inner regions of the galaxies.

The discussed theory mainly utilizes mathematical spaces from stochastic analysis and allows for the application of limit theorems to dependent random elements across time. A recent publication by Kandita and Van der Meulen (2021) established dependence-based tail dependence estimates for traditional stoping times, and our work builds upon this by expanding the possible stopping times to incorporate non-traditional times. These new results yield additional generalizations of the mentioned estimates.

We investigate the optical properties of T centre ensembles in diamond to better understand their potential applications in quantum technology. Our analysis focuses on the unique spectral characteristics of T centres, including their absorption, emission, and scattering properties, and how these properties are affected by the environment and temperature. Leveraging our understanding of T centre dynamics, we explain the observed spectral features and corresponding timescales, and how they may be influenced by vacuum fields and other environmental factors to different degrees in various settings. Our research also enables the development of a practical tool that can predict the spectral characteristics of T centres under various conditions. By expanding on previous work, we update the optical properties of T centres to account for recent findings and clarify the relationships between their optical properties.

This research focuses on developing an automated approach to identify breast tumors in mammography images. The method combines morphological analysis and region growing technique to pinpoint the tumors. First, the approach filters out noise in the image using the morphological analysis, and subsequently, the region growing technique is employed to mark the tumors. A simple yet effective classification system based on the shape and size of the identified marks is devised to categorize them as tumors or non-tumors. The performance of this system is evaluated using real mammography images, and the results indicate a high accuracy and reliability for its application in a clinical setting.

This study explores the relationship between degenerate Bernoulli numbers, circulant matrices, and finite fields through Gauss hypergeometric functions and sums of powers of integers in a polynomial ring. We establish a general formula for degenerate Bernoulli numbers, examine their connection to the values of the Gauss hypergeometric function at certain rational arguments, and express this relationship in terms of circulant matrices that combine the powers of integers in a polynomial ring and take into account the characteristics of the base field. Furthermore, we derive explicit formulas for various degrees of degenerate Bernoulli numbers, confirming initial conjectures proposed by other researchers. Our approach also enables us to provide an alternative proof for the divisibility of certain Bernoulli numbers by prime powers.

The task of minimizing radial velocity jitter in line lists has been tackled using a randomized approach, and our study validates its effectiveness. We employ a statistical test to compare the results of randomly selecting lines from a spectrum to those chosen based on a parametric model, and our analysis shows the randomized method produces significantly fewer noisy lines. Additionally, the randomized approach allows for a increased line density, resulting in a greater reduction in radial velocity jitter. A increased line density in line lists may have significant implications for the construction of large spectroscopic surveys.

This research paper proposes a technique called Hierarchical Range Sectoring (HRS) to minimize the number of hidden terminals in wireless sensor networks. The concept of HRS is an adaptation of the standard range-division technique, applied across multiple hierarchy levels. The algorithm calculates each level's data transmission interval and corresponding range/sector size, determined by aggregate time intervals from all lower levels. The HRS approach dynamic optimization method considers each level's unique characteristics, such as data transmission patterns and available bandwidth, to calculate range/sector sizes. The HRS approach dynamic optimization method considers each level's unique characteristics, such as data transmission patterns and available bandwidth, to calculate range/sector sizes. The HRS is designed to operate across various wireless communication technologies and is impartial to specific physical layer characteristics. Through comprehensive simulations, HRS demonstrates significant reductions in packet loss, latency, and improved network throughput.

Deep neural network-based object detectors have been intensely researched and
implemented in diverse scenarios. While initial focus was on developing
state-of-the-art detection performance, contemporary work is starting to
examine the underlying reasons behind the success of these object detectors.
Researchers are studying the inherent properties of object detectors, their
behavior in response to varying image resolution, and their performance with
modified outputs. In this work, we investigate how different object detectors
behave when used in a variety of situations, including with altered input
images, changed output feature grid sizes, and non-standard training images.
We evaluated six popular object detectors across three diverse evaluation
scenarios, finding significant performance variations. Our study demonstrates the
importance of selecting the appropriate object detector based on its intended
use and highlights the need for standardized evaluation protocols in the
object detection community. We have open-sourced our experimental framework,
referred to as the TackleDet toolkit, which enables automated object detector
evaluation in diverse scenarios.

We have investigated a class of quasilinear elliptic systems under specific growth conditions on the functions f_i, which satisfy the condition |f_i(u)| = o(|u|^{p_i-2}) as |u| tends to zero. By establishing an auxiliary result, we have shown that for a certain range of parameters, there exists a positive solution to the given system in the context of bounded domains in R^n. Additionally, we have obtained a ground state solution when p_i = 2 for all i, and a solution with compact support when p_i > 2 for all i, without the restriction of being in the space H^1_0. Notably, the condition |f_i(u)| = o(|u|^{p_i-2}) as |u| tends to zero allows us to handle a broader range of parameters than existing literature, and this development marks a significant advancement in the study of supercritical systems with definite potentials.

We establish concise concentration inequalities for the sum of multiple independent Bernoulli variables, conditional on this sum being equal to a specific value $k$. These inequalities apply to both convex functions and polynomial functions of $k$. Our primary tool is a generalized version of the Bousquet-Ruscol-Gentil (BGG) inequality, which includes the original BGG inequality as a special case. Our findings specifically yield: - A simplified and more transparent proof of the concentrated upper bound for Bernoulli variables, conditional on their sum being equal to $k$, with an improved constant of $\min(1/(3N),1/2)$, where $N$ represents the number of Bernoulli variables. This result can be extended to independent, non-identically distributed variables. - More precise bounds for the concentrated upper bound, conditional on the sum being equal to $k$, with improved constants of $\min(1/(3N_i),1/2)$ for variables with different probabilities of success. - Generalized inequalities for the concentrated upper bound, conditional on the sum being equal to $k$, with improved constants of $\min(1/(3N(p_u)),1/2)$ for variables with different probabilities of success, where $N(p_u)$ represents the total number of variables with the probability of success $p_u$. - Upper bounds for the probability of a low-value outcome, conditional on the sum being equal to $k$, with improved constants of $\min(1

This research investigates the relationship between the torsion crystalline cohomology and étale cohomology of a scheme, using the context of perfect rings with a fixed set of Witt vectors. By establishing an analog of the Beilinson's Conjecture, the study connects the torsion crystalline cohomology to the torsion étale cohomology for schemes over such rings, demonstrating a reciprocal correspondence between the two types of cohomology. Additionally, the investigation demonstrates that this relationship holds for Hilbert modular varieties, specifically showing that the torsion crystalline cohomology captures the same information as the torsion étale cohomology about the geometry of these varieties.

This paper delves into the measurement of the charge of the recoil hadron asymmetry in collisions at 9.96 TeV, where final states consisting of a charmed meson and a recoil hadron are examined. The goal is to investigate the dihadron fragmentation function, specifically when the charmed meson is produced, and the measurement of the asymmetry is sensitive to this fragmention process. To analyze the data, a four-particle system is constructed using the decay products of the charmed meson and the recoil hadron, and the asymmetry is calculated on a event-by-event basis for the data and for the charmed meson distribution without considering the recoil hadron system. The measurement shows a non-zero asymmetry for events within a certain invariant mass range and shows agreement with theoretical predictions that take into account the dihadron fragmentation function and the distribution of the charmed meson. The measurement also shows a larger than expected asymmetry for events above the given mass range and indicates the need for additional understanding of the charmed meson distribution in this higher energy range.

In this work, the nature of the concept of invariant length within the context of the de Sitter spacetime is reexamined through the lens of the Fock transformation. Our analysis reveals that the relationship between the invariant length and the spacetime dimensions holds constant at approximately 4.3+1 or 5-dimensional configurations. This finding challenges the common assumption in the literature that the concept of length remains unaffected in 5-dimensional de Sitter spacetime. Instead, we show that the Fock transformation can be an dependable tool for exploring the properties of the de Sitter spacetime, enabling us to comprehend the behavior of particles within this environment and make accurate predictions for processes such as particle scattering.

Let's consider the special symplectic group $Sp_{2m}(q)$ from the perspective of its conjugacy classes. We have developed a comprehensive system of invariants that enables us to distinctively identify all conjugacy classes and calculate their respective sizes. This system is comprised of two types of quadratic and hermitian forms, specifically $m$ forms of type I, II, or III, depending on the underlying field and its characteristics. Given this system's properties and our previous work on $Sp_{2m}(q)$, we can explore various classification-related topics, such as classifying conjugacy classes based on their associated non-degenerate quadratic or hermitian forms, determining the maximum possible size of a conjugacy class, and establishing the equivalence between two elements' conjugacy classes depending on a specific bilinear form being isotropic.

Recommendation systems rely on entity representations to suggest relevant items to users. These representations can be both accurate and practical if entities are viewed as combined topological and semantic structures. By leveraging the interconnected recommendations within a structure and the inherent meaning associated with an entity, we can develop a collaborative filtering model that incorporates both topological and semantic aspects. In this paper, we present an approach called TopoSMC, which combines topology and content in entity representations to enhance their effectiveness. Our proposed method, TopoSMC, uses a collaborative filtering model that incorporates both semantic mean and topological spatial temporal convolutional layers to process topological and semantic structures in recommendation tasks. Our experimental results show that our proposed TopoSMC model surpasses state-of-the-art collaborative filtering models in recommending structurally complex entities, such as images with objects, where entity structures are defined by both object classification and bounding boxes.

In evaluating whether a patient should accept an incompatible kidney offer, decision-makers weigh the benefits of transplantation against the costs of delaying further treatment. We develop an mathematical framework for Kidney Exchange Networks by incorporating incompatibility as a state variable in Markov Decision Processes. This allows us to examine how patients make acceptance decisions under uncertainty. Our analysis reveals common features in optimal policies and demonstrates the significant impact of network structure on waiting times, revealing both local and global patterns in decision-making behavior. Finally, we highlight the practical implications of our findings for understanding strategic interactions in kidney transplantation networks.

The Bayesian perspective on estimating copula parameters is a powerful method that enables a comprehensive comparison of different models based on their underlying structures. A key aspect of this approach involves the use of prior distributions to penetrate the copula's complex surface, allowing for the interpretation of parameters in a statistically meaningful way. In our research, we delve into a series of innovative Bayesian methods for estimating parameters in two primary categories of copulas: their core structures (such as the Gaussian and Bi-Parametric structures) and their composite forms (such as the Student-T and Mixted copulas). We conduct an in-depth analysis of how these methods affect the estimation of parameters, and provide a detailed comparison of their performance using simulated data sets and real-world applications, along with a comprehensive overview of the relevant theoretical foundations.

High-dimensional data with numerous dimensions poses challenges for visual analysis. A common solution involves reducing dimensionality through Word2Vec embeddings, which map words to vectors that capture their semantic relationships. However, these embeddings can be misleading when applied to certain word pairs, such as antonyms, that are commonly misinterpreted as similar in meaning. This is particularly problematic in fields like finance, where accurate information is crucial, and where certain words like "bubble" and "burst" have distinct meanings. Our goal in this research is to explore the effectiveness of using Word2Vec embeddings to reduce dimensionality for financial data, specifically utilizing pre-trained vectors and assessing the results in various dimensions. Our findings show that while these embeddings are beneficial in certain situations, they can also lead to unexpected outcomes, such as incorrectly classifying companies that are in a bubble as those whose stocks will quickly recover. This research provides a starting point for future studies seeking to validate the use of these embeddings in financial contexts.

In next-generation wireless networks, the process of forming waves is critical to creating high-throughput and fair connections. The goal is to allocate resources in such a way that maximizes the total throughput and ensures a minimum acceptable throughput for each connection. This paper explores the concept of waveforming through an optimization process and proposes a non-cooperative game framework to determine a fair and efficient outcome. The proposed approach ensures that each connection has the opportunity to influence the outcome and make informed decisions based on its own requirements and preferences. The paper also establishes the stability of the game by proving that each connection has a dominant strategy that leads to a purified equilibrium in a specific scenario. The proposed framework can be applied to optimize both fair-throughput and sum-throughput objectives. The article concludes by highlighting the potential of waveforming as an innovative technique to create high-performance wireless networks.

A continuous, linearly expanding wave pattern deformities were modeled after the Rayleigh--B\'enard instability occurrence using a mixture of micro-and macroscopic model adjustments. Thermocausal turbulence theory was employed to develop a two-tiered model comprising thermocausal surface layer and turbulent inner layer. The model includes an expanding wave pattern-derived instability source within the turbulent inner layer. It is shown that the proposed model results in an oscillatory wave pattern and potentially linear expansion wave pattern. Additionally, the model predicts an instability growth rate increase and natural frequency decrease with expanding wave pattern speed. Notably, the model distinguishes between primary instability waves and secondary turbulence-driven expansion waves. The relationship between the wave pattern speed and the expansion rate is defined by an instability-induced equation. This paper introduces an innovative interpretation method for formal language rules, specifically designed to tackle the challenge of ambiguous syntactic analyses. Existing interpretation techniques often yield multiple possible meanings for a single sentence due to the cyclic nature of parsing. In contrast, our proposed method involves a unique, carefully tailored interpretation of the tree structure that yields a single, well-defined meaning for each sentence, even if its syntactic analysis is ambiguous. In building this method, we leveraged insights gained from uncovering the underlying patterns in human interpretations of language expressions. Our interpretation approach takes a more subjective view of meaning and represents it as a function that takes in linguistic rules and the structure of a given expression, or sentence. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through experiments showing that machine-generated interpretations of expressions vary little compared to human-generated ones, and that human-generated interpretations exhibit significant variation when the underlying expression structure is altered. We further show that human interpretations follow a probability distribution that is distinct from the one assumed in traditional parsing models. In assessing our method, we introduce a metric called symmetric difference, which indicates that a substantial portion of human interpretations of expression structures differ from the predicted outcomes according to our proposed model. Nonetheless, our method still achieves notable performance in this regard. We hope that through these findings and the introduction of our subjectivist interpretation approach, we can spark further discussion on the nature of meaning in language.

In collaborative settings, players can decline actions that lead to a worse outcome, leading to the emergence of a more robust concept known as iteratively dominated actions. This paper explores the challenge of teaching players to shun these actions through a process of trial and error in complex, dynamic environments shared by multiple agents. We test this learning capacity with a scalable multi-agent learning platform, where players must reduce the adverse effects of their actions on a shared resource affected by noise and changes in a random environment. The results show that a technique called evolutionary algorithm enhances learning performance by a significant amount, with an average improvement of about 2.5 times over baseline models in this demanding test scenario.

In an emerging model, relationships among a group of people are modeled as connected nodes in a random network. At specific, regularly occurring time intervals, a few connections are randomly changed, simulating how social connections typically shift in daily life. When a highly contagious disease breaks out in this community, the model is used to study how the number of individuals infected evolves over time. The model focuses on two different time scales: short periods, during which a few connections are changed, and long periods, during which the infection spreads and many connections change. The model predicts that the ultimate peak in the number of infected individuals will increase indefinitely if the network is restarted repeatedly, under both theoretical and practical conditions. Additionally, the speed at which the infection spreads will increase over time and, on average, the peak will occur at roughly half the speed of infection. The model was also verified through simulations and the findings compare favorably to previous models. The speed at which the infection spreads accelerates as the number of individuals with connections increases, but slows down in a completely random connection structure. The model reveals that the ultimate peak in the number of infected individuals will continue to increase without limit in a completely random structure, but will eventually reach a limit in a more organized structure. The model predicts that the peak will occur more frequently towards the beginning of the epidemic. The model also shows that restarting the network from different initial conditions produces similar results. The findings compare favorably to previous models and provide new insights.
