We investigate Cotton solitons in 3-dimensional manifolds with Reeb vector fields that are not orthogonal to the associated potential vector fields. Initially, we determine the geometric characteristics of these solitons in complex 3-$h$-manifolds. Then, we demonstrate the invariance of the solitons' geometry when the Reeb vector field changes direction. Building on this, we show that in 3-$h$-manifolds, the steady Cotton solitons with the potential vector field orthogonal to the Reeb vector field define $SU(2)$-invariant, torsion-free $N$-metrics. This expands our understanding of the subject, which previously only included minimal surfaces and ODE-defined metrics. The research also reveals that the associated vector fields satisfy specific compatibility conditions, leading to the closure of the complexified soliton vectors in the complexified tangent space. This complex closure implies the presence of a holomorphic minimal surface when the potential vector field changes direction. The study further demonstrates that the oriented 3-$h$-manifolds whose Reeb vector fields change direction have a global, steerable, and minimal surface when the associated vector fields are in the direction of the complex part of the complexified Reeb vector field. This finding expands on previous research that only applied to locally defined minimal surfaces.

The Drell-Yan rapidity differential at any scale can be represented by a set of integral equations, which evolve parton distribution functions (PDFs) according to the DGLAP framework. These equations form a solvable system for a given rapidity range, enabling the extraction of PDFs at any scale through global fits, assuming the DGLAP evolution holds. Nevertheless, at scales beyond the typical range of PDF datasets (around a few tens of GeV), the accuracy of these extracts becomes uncertain. A new approach has been developed to directly determine PDFs from global datasets, bypassing the evolution to the desired scale. This method, based on the evolution of unfolded distributions, allows for a more precise determination of PDFs at high energies and can be applied to various processes, powered by theoretical calculations of observable cross-sections in terms of PDFs.

The standard experience replay method is a key component in deep reinforcement learning, but it has a significant shortcoming: the lack of variance reduction. This limitation is addressed by a new VRER framework, which leverages a representation of the target function to guide the sampling of experiences and obtain a more accurate policy gradient estimate. The paper then introduces a novel algorithm within this framework, incorporating a functional representation learned through neural networks to compute an optimal sampling distribution that directly yields a policy gradient. The algorithm is shown to converge to an optimal solution under mild assumptions, and numerical examples demonstrate its effectiveness and flexibility. The paper also examines the trade-offs between using optimal sampling and the benefits of reducing variance through a deeper analysis of the computational costs involved. The findings suggest that the proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art deep reinforcement learning methods and provide valuable insights into the VRER framework. The code for the algorithms considered in the paper is available online.

The libcommute library, initially created by the University of Oregon's Research group led by Ira B. Fletcher, has been enhanced with Python 3 bindings, making its symbolic algebra capabilities more versatile and accessible to a broader range of users. Originally designed to support the development of the AEGIS protocol, a quantum communication method, this update is relevant to the expansion of AEGIS to higher-dimensional systems and its implementation on ion trap quantum devices.

Using high-bias precision spectroscopy, we've discovered a significant superconducting gap at the zone corner in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ single crystals, which is surprisingly large, exceeding the usual 2$\Delta$$_{max}$/k$_{B}$T$_{c}$ ratio. This unusually sized gap at the zone corner may contribute to the complex normal-state behavior in this class of materials. Our findings also reveal the existence of nodal and nodal-less states near the superconducting transition temperature in (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$, showing that the nodal state can persist up to 88% of T$_c$. This is in contrast to the nodal-less state found in (Ba$_{0.85}$K$_{0.15}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ using high-resolution laser spectroscopy, and highlights the varying nodal structures that can occur in iron-based superconductors.

We establish a precise equivalence between the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula by employing the diagrammatic technique of bosonized diagrams. This equivalence demonstration holds for all types of Hubbard-Stratonovich transformations, including those that are approximate. As a result, we reobtain the superbosonization formula through the perspective of the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, gaining further understanding of its underlying physics. This equivalence also allows us to derive explicit renormalization group transformations for the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation by relating them to the RG flows of the BCS-type interactions in the process of bosonization. Consequently, we can investigate the stability of the phase transition driven by the BCS-type interactions under various conditions.

Initial findings from the LHCb experiment at the European Organization for Nuclear Research by detecting top quark production from single hadron decays are reported, utilizing data at 13 TeV and corresponding to over 80 billion recorded events. Top quark properties, specifically spin asymmetry and differential distribution in lateral direction for decays into $B$-mesons, were calculated with precision reaching 0.24 and 0.053 respectively, showing alignment with standard model expectations.

LaNiO$_3$ superlattices with varying LaNiO$_3$ thickness were investigated to understand how the thickness affects the temperature-dependent conductivity. Conductivity measurements in these materials showed two relaxation components with distinct temperature dependences. The faster relaxing component's temperature dependence changes from positive to negative as LaNiO$_3$ thickness increases beyond 2 units, and this threshold is attributed to an interface-related phenomenon. As LaNiO$_3$ thickness increases, the conducting effectiveness of LaNiO$_3$ interfaces decreases due to increased nickel valence, and this effect is linked to the formation of extra valence states in nickel atoms at the interface. These extra valence states cause an opposition to conductivity, and this resistance can be both resistant to and facilitated by temperature changes, resulting in the observed bi-temporal conductivity response. A 10-unit LaNiO$_3$ layer exhibits typical LaNiO$_3$ conductivity, and this conductivity is driven by both tunneling and hopping mechanisms. The study provides insight into the conductive properties of LaNiO$_3$ when it's part of a superlattice.

To understand the complex behaviors of highly advanced conversational artificial intelligence, it is necessary to grasp its ability to comprehend others' perspectives. While some have questioned the necessity of this perspective-taking ability, research shows that humans naturally associate it with conversational intelligence. A well-designed experiment was conducted to examine the relationship between this ability and advanced language skills, with participants generating realistic dialogue scenarios. The results revealed a significant connection between perspective-taking and abilities to both recognize and anticipate others' thoughts, as well as a weaker connection to predicting their own thoughts. Interestingly, the relationship between perspective-taking and these skills varied depending on the part of speech used. In contrast to previous findings, the data showed no connection between perspective-taking and the generation of overall coherence. These findings provide valuable insights into the capabilities and limitations of advanced language skills and offer a method for evaluating the cognitive aspects of artificial intelligence through human-generated data.

To assess the average capacity of a wireless communication system that uses the capabilities of meta-surfaces to enhance performance, we develop a mathematical model that accounts for the behavior of multiple independent Rayleigh fading channels and corresponding reflection coefficients under co-directional phase shifts. Our approach allows for general meta-surface sizes, and our analysis reveals that correlated fading and reflection coefficients can significantly impact capacity by creating both beneficial and detrimental effects that are tied to the size of the network. Furthermore, we verify the validity of our model by comparing it to simulations and utilize it to demonstrate the effectiveness of a matched filtering technique that enhances capacity by a factor of up to four, depending on the network size and the strength of the signal.

MG-GLAM, a cutting-edge N-body simulation code for investigating the dynamics of massive, gravitationally bound systems in an expanding and cooling universe, has been developed. This code is based on the Lagrange-Taylor formalism and utilizes look-up tables to model the behavior of a comprehensive set of atomic and molecular species commonly found in molecular clouds. By integrating the principles of hierarchical structure and multiple time-stepping methods, MG-GLAM is designed for high performance computing and can perform complex N-body simulations efficiently while accurately modeling real-world celestial environments.

We derive a parameterized family of growth models for planar domains with curved boundaries in the upper half-plane, which includes the chordal LE Wyner–Briggs process, LE Wong–Sherman process, and LE Yang--Zhang process as special cases. By connecting these models to the Schramm--Loewener evolution and the Loewener equation, we demonstrate they minimize the power of which the Lebesgue measure on the real line is carried by the corresponding boundary function. This mathematical expression represents the geometric concept of'slit surfaces' in complex analysis. It is also shown that the Loewener equation can be solved using the Lebesgue measure carried by the domain's boundary function. This solution involves the parametrized family of surfaces, which can be used to establish connections between these models and other processes, such as the LE Wyner--Briggs process with independent increments and the LE Wong--Sherman process with independent increments and bounded boundaries. It is found that the speed of growth for all these processes is proportional to the square of the L^2 norm of the Loewener operator applied to the domain's boundary function.

This paper introduces WorkingWiki, a high-tech version of the basic wiki
platform commonly used for managing manuscripts and software projects. Like
traditional wikis, WorkingWiki relies on version control systems to keep
track of changes, but it also incorporates cutting-edge web technologies to
create interactive content and utilize data visualization to present results.

The linearized model's applicability and stability in modeling turbulent reactive flows was tested, and it was determined that the 'eddy breakdown' model of combustion is the most compatible with the linearized framework. This model was found to be equivalent to the 'progress variable' model, and a modified form of the linearized equations was used to analyze wave propagation in a turbulent jet with multiple reaction zones. Numerical solutions to the modified equations revealed how different parameters affect the dispersion and absorption of waves, and approximate analytical expressions were derived to describe this behavior in jets with weak turbulent mixing.

Researchers have long been fascinated by the internal waves that occur within stars and the way they affect their behavior. These waves are influenced by the star's gravitational pull and its buoyant nature, and it is only recently, with the advent of highly accurate measurements, that it has been possible to study them in detail. A new study uses data from the K2 spacecraft to examine these waves within the Kepler stars and finds a consistent pattern of behavior that was previously predicted by theoretical models. The findings show that the stars' acoustic-buoyant frequency plays a crucial role in determining the types of waves that form across different energy levels. The discovery could lead to a better understanding of how these waves behave in other types of stars and even in stars that have already exploded as supernovae.

The long-term behavior of nonlinear systems functioning within an environment of external influences can be complex, as observed in systems that rely on multiple interacting clusters for synchronization. However, identifying the number of these clusters can be challenging due to the system's reduced dimensionality and the presence of irregular behavior. In this research, a method is introduced to determine the number of clusters in a dynamical system relying on synchronization, by applying a novel approach to simplify the system and reduce its dimensionality. This method is demonstrated through application to a van der Pol oscillator in an external acoustic field, with results showing a cluster of two clusters existing for specific frequency conditions, which is verified through numerical simulation and theoretical stability analysis.

We investigate the dynamics of nearest-neighbor coupled variables on different geometrical configurations, specifically triadic and diamond lattice structures, in the context of self-organized criticality. The triadic structure, obtained by dividing each unit into three equal parts, represents a universal framework for studying variable-sized systems. In contrast, the diamond lattice structure, derived from the hexagonal lattice by replacing each bond with a diamond-shaped structure, represents a unique case of variable-sized interactions. Our study reveals a common feature in both triadic and diamond lattice dynamics: the occurrence of distinct, synchronized oscillations of different sizes. As size increases in the triadic structure and in the inner rings of the diamond lattice, the time of oscillation notably decreases. Additionally, a significant finding in the diamond lattice is the discovery of an irregular, scale-free behavior in the outer rings. Furthermore, our analysis of the triadic and diamond lattices using the concept of variable sizes leads to a more comprehensive understanding of corresponding dynamics on hexagonal and square lattices, showcasing how variable-sized systems exhibit a broader spectrum of oscillatory and irregular behaviors.

Researchers suggest that ultralight dark matter, in the form of a scalar field, could make up the majority of the universe's mass and is connected to a neutrino mass term. This theory was analyzed in a model that incorporates a cosmological phase transition and nontypical initial conditions for the scalar field. The study reveals the implications of this relationship on neutrino behavior during big bang nucleosynthesis and in subsequent cosmic environments. The research also examines the possibilities for detecting this type of dark matter through observations of galaxy spectra and neutrino experiments. The findings indicate that even if this dark matter is present, it may not significantly influence big bang nucleosynthesis or the stability of the universe. However, the existence of this dark matter could lead to additional modes of neutrino decay, which may affect the production of certain elements during future nucleosynthesis processes. The study also shows that a neutrino dark matter model can result in the formation of a stable, planet-mass object at the center of the universe, potentially explaining the monopole problem. Furthermore, even if this dark matter is not produced, the universe could still be composed of a type of dark energy driven by a scalar field connected to the neutrino mass term.

We investigate the concept of 'cosmic ray ensembles,' which refers to unusually large groups of cosmic rays with similar origins and direction. These ensembles are anticipated to originate from extremely energetic and remotely situated Ultra High Energy (UHE) photons that have induced air showers on Earth's path. If our theory is correct, it's possible that future large-scale cosmic ray experiments might observe these ensembles, which could provide insights into the nature of these UHE photons. We developed an statistical model to create realistic groups of cosmic rays based on their energy and arrival directions, which can be compared to actual data sets to indirectly offer information about the parameters of the UHE photons involved, specifically their arrival direction, energy range, and density. This could be especially useful in exploring the nature of these UHE photons, as a direct detection of them is extremely challenging due to the vast distances involved.

A nonlocal theory of gravity has been proposed, with a constitutive relation derived from an asymptotically safe framework in $d=2$ dimensions. This relation is expressed in terms of the nonlocal parameter $\Lambda$ and the mesoscopic scale $k$, and it matches the conventional weak-field expression for Newton's constant. The proposed theory predicts a change in the relationship between $G(N)$ and $k$, which could be confirmed by experimental measurements of gravitational forces at mesoscopic scales. In addition to this, the nonlocal theory generates an extra, universal potential with a range determined by $\Lambda$, which could be identified by analyzing the motion of planetary orbits over a period of about $10^7$ years. The estimated value of $\Lambda$ is found to be $k \approx 10^{-3}$ eV, which may be related to the existence of a cosmological constant. The introduction of matter nonlocality is shown to result in an interaction between the intrinsic and extrinsic curvatures, leading to an additional contribution to the dark energy density. The total nonlocal density consists of the intrinsic component $\rho_{\rm intr} = \rho/4\pi\Lambda^2$ and the extrinsic component $\rho_{\rm extr} = \rho_{\rm DE} - \rho_{\rm intr}$. The relationship between $\rho_{\rm intr}$ and $\rho_{\rm extr}$ is determined by the extrinsic curvature

Autonomous distributed systems require a different approach to manage data consistently and efficiently, making Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) an essential element for the reliable development of distributed applications. However, creating a CRDT specification for a new application can be very challenging and error-prone, as it necessitates a thorough understanding of both the data model and the replication algorithm. Currently, there are various design frameworks for CRDTs, but they often lack formal specifications and have implicit assumptions, potentially leading to unexpected behavior in specific scenarios. To address this issue, we present a formal design framework called Quark for specifying CRDTs and ensuring the consistency and efficiency of distributed data. Quark leverages the established terminology from the research community on CRDTs and introduces a clear distinction between the data model, operation system, replication algorithm, and safety properties to provide a comprehensive and easily maintainable framework for developing CRDTs. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we applied Quark to create specifications for prominent CRDT examples, including last seen values, multi-sets, counters, and vector clocks, and have made these specifications available for public reference. Furthermore, Quark can be used in conjunction with automated verification tools to analyze the design specifications and ensure that the intended safety properties are upheld.

We explored the relationship between protein sequences and genetic variants that affect phenotypes, noting significant discrepancies in influence across different traits. Our analysis revealed that protein sequences have the greatest impact on immune response, metabolism, and development-related genes, whereas coding regions with minimal functional insight are more likely to be associated with miscellaneous functions. We observed that certain variants with a significant impact on protein sequences are often found in distant locations along the genome, indicating that their placement may be optimized for structural properties rather than sequence-based functionality. We further found that variants influencing protein sequences are more likely to be found in exons than introns, with a higher proportion located in 5' UTR and 3' UTR regions than expected. Approximately half of the variants affecting protein structures are situated near specific amino acids known as 'hotspots', which exhibit a heightened capacity for absorbing and distorting the energy associated with structural changes. We found that certain 'hotspot' amino acids are more prone to being located at the surface, embedded within helices, or positioned near flexible regions in human proteins. We found substantial variability in the distribution of 'hotspot' amino acids across different protein families and found that certain variants affecting these key residues may contribute to the etiology of certain diseases. We identified numerous examples of SNPs with a significant effect on protein sequences that may be worth further analysis in the context of their functional implications. The LHC proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV have been studied by the ALICE experiment to examine the production of particles with strange quarks in final states characterized by mid-rapidity multiplicity.  Investigated particle species include $\phi$, $K^*$, $\Lambda$, $\Sigma^0$, $\Xi$, and $\Omega$.  Results show that the yield ratios of these strange particles to corresponding non-strange particles rely on charged particle pairs in a manner consistent with previous ATLAS and CMS findings, yet differ significantly from theoretical models predicting an increase in strangeness with rising multiplicity.  Also, an enhanced production of strange particles observed at high multiplicities is supported by several theoretical concepts, including the possibility of an increase in parton densities and a strangeness enhancement due to interactions between particles and the medium, as observed in higher-energy heavy-ion experiments.  Furthermore, the measured $\phi$ to $\Lambda$ ratio provides insight into the composition of the quark-glue phase transition proposed in multiphase chaos theory.

The number of known neutron star Low Mass X-ray Binaries and millisecond radio pulsars is significant, but exactly how they relate to each other remains unclear. To tackle this question, we used data from the International Gamma-Ray Astrophysics Laboratory's complete all-sky map and the Parkes Radio Survey, setting a minimum for the detection of sources at 2 times the background threshold. Our analysis yielded 29 LMXB candidates, 9 of which are associated with gamma-ray sources, and 85 MSP candidates, 9 of which are linked to LMXBs. To estimate the total populations of these systems, we employed Poisson regression on spatial and orbital periods, finding a possible 70 LMXBs and 480 MSPs in the Galaxy. These numbers suggest that the majority of millisecond pulsars are part of an interacting population, but further study is needed to confirm this conclusion.

Using line velocities from the APOGEE-2 and the LAMO surveys, the velocities of 77 wide binary stars were determined, enabling the calculation of one-dimensional velocity dispersion for five specific frequency ranges. To derive these velocities, a line list was created for each star, consisting of typically 20 to 30 lines, with a minimum wavelength of 5,000Å and a maximum at 2,500Å, for which the stellar parameters were relatively consistent, having an RMS of 0.04 in [Fe/H] and 0.075 in [Fe/H]. The line velocities were determined through the use of multiple techniques, including the implementation of line lists by itself, line lists in conjunction with stellar parameters, line profiles, and line sets defined by spectral types. Utilizing a systematic approach, the line velocities were found to be an average of 0.16km/s more accurate than star-to-star measurements. This enhancement in line velocity accuracy, resulting from the inclusion of line data, led to a velocity dispersion two times more accurate in wide binary star systems. This improvement, however, does not significantly impact the current understanding of wide binary star systems. A velocity dispersion of approximately 1.5 to 2.7 km/s was calculated for each of the five specific energy ranges. These measurements are comparable to recent findings from the LAMO survey and a study of local wide binary stars. A binary motion test was also developed to compare observed line widths with those

The relationship between the polarization of radio sources and the curvature of the radio spectrum remains poorly understood. To gain insight into this phenomenon, we examined the polarization properties of extragalactic radio sources at frequencies between 0.1 and 2.0 GHz, using data from the International Giant Meterwave Radio Telescope Survey and the Sydney University Radio Sky Survey. Our analysis reveals a notable correlation between the polarization fraction and wavelength-dependent behavior in the radio spectrum, with a significant impact on the distribution of sources based on their curvature. We find that sources with more rapid curvature exhibit higher polarization fractions, and our findings suggest a connection between highly polarized sources and the presence of compact synergetic galaxies. These results provide a starting point for a comprehensive study of the relationship between the radio spectrum and polarization fraction across various source classes.

The issue of weak shocks stabilizing into strong shocks has been resolved, and evidence shows this transition occurs rapidly, at the shock front itself, through a local explosion, without the need for viscous or heat transfer effects across the shock. This behavior was initially observed in a one-dimensional gas with a power-law index greater than one and now has been expanded to include other complex explosions in one, two, and three dimensions. Additionally, this research reveals that in gases with memory and dispersion effects, explosive behavior can result in shocks transitioning from weak to strong, and it is demonstrated that these strong shocks can persist even in an infinite, one-dimensional gas with memory and dispersion properties.

We make a significant discovery regarding the geometric modularity of rank 2 sheaves under the influence of multiple algebraic weights. Our research indicates that these weights can contribute to geometric modularity in non-algebraic weights. This finding builds upon the concepts introduced in the papers by J. Laumon and B. Rybhansmi, and simplifies the conditions required for geometric modularity, particularly for Ginzburg automorphisms and Hecke algebras. Additionally, our work facilitates the application of geometric modularity to rank 2 sheaves across various ground fields and residue characteristics.

Chemical reactions can be complex, with multiple vibrational degrees of freedom that complicate control over sensitive energy barriers. Despite this challenge, research on the active control of chemical reactions using infrared light has shown promising progress. Empirical findings suggest that in some molecules, specific vibrational modes can be manipulated to influence reaction rates, implying a potential for more efficient photochemical energy conversion. This discovery motivates the investigation of novel quantum architectures that integrate photonic vibrational control, where light is used to drive chemical reactions through precise adjustments to energy barriers. Using the H$_2$AB$_2$ molecule as an example, we demonstrate that incorporating vibrational degrees of freedom into its quantum simulation enhances the control over its reaction barrier when subjected to intense laser fields. Our analysis highlights the potential of this approach to optimize photochemical energy conversion in complex molecules.

Adachi, Iyama, and Reiten's breakthrough work introduced $\tau$-tilting theory, a profound extension of the classical Klondike theorem. Prior to its development, Basso, Iyama, and Keller independently discovered the underlying principles, allowing for expansion of $\tau$-tilting theory to $a_u$-tilting theory. This introduction leads to the derivation of enhanced Miyamoto identities and the $\tau$-orbit theorem.

To enable natural user interactions, dialogue systems must effectively employ both content and semantic variety in their responses. While numerous approaches have been developed to enhance content diversity, fewer focus on semantic variety and response quality. Our proposed framework, which combines a diversity-promoting dialogue model and a response evaluation model based on reinforcement learning, aims to address this limitation. By incorporating a diversity-promoting loss function and a response evaluation model in the closed loop of reinforcement learning, our framework encourages the generation of semantically diverse and high-quality responses. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms baseline methods in terms of content and semantic variety, as well as response quality, as measured by user studies.

Automated driving relies heavily on software components that must be highly reliable. To ensure their stability, revising these components regularly is essential to update them according to new guidelines and to fix any existing issues. Unfortunately, maintaining them can be time-consuming and costly. Thus, a collaborative approach between the development and testing teams is desired to accelerate this process. Unfortunately, a common performance metric is often used to trigger costly re-testing, leading to a substantial burden on the testing team. To overcome this challenge, this study proposes a machine learning-based quality prediction framework, referred to as QualityPredict. It identifies areas of the code that require testing to be performed quickly and efficiently, reducing the testing time significantly. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, a real-world example from the open-source Autoware development project is utilized, showing that the proposed framework accelerates the testing process by 15 times. Additionally, this approach is found to improve the overall development cycle time by 24%.

If a substellar object with a mass less than 0.6 times the mass of the sun experiences hydrogen burning through helium flash or mixed-mode oscillations, the process occurs at an angular momentum threshold, exceeding which would lead to catastrophic consequences. However, our research indicates that this threshold is surpassed at the angular momentum values typical for fully conserved orbits in binary systems. Utilizing the eggcarton equation, a geometric approach was developed to represent angular momentum boundaries in a binary system, a scenario that includes highly eccentric orbits. Our model reveals that the angular momentum boundary for instability in an eggcarton potential is identical to that found with numerical simulations. A simplified approach was also derived to estimate the marginally stable eccentricities for highly stable eccentric orbits. These models provide clear, easily visualized guidelines for determining the angular momentum requirements for stability in eggcarton potentials, including scenarios involving close approaches or distant orbits.

To facilitate measurements of hadron decay rates, an artificial neural network can be trained to estimate the primary decay particle's energy from the total final energy in BaBar's dimensionality-reduced data. This network will be sensitive to variations in energy estimation, thereby enabling the simultaneous extraction of hadron decay rates and energy scales for BaBar's dataset. A method for assessing the scale's uncertainty through artificial neural network sensitivity is introduced and demonstrated with an accuracy of less than one percent.

We introduce a general, semi-analytical formula to estimate afterglows of Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) in diverse relativistic and non-relativistic scenarios. This model's novelty lies in its unified approach, applicable across the spectrum from ultra-relativistic to non-relativistic phases, and is hence dubbed the "Universal Afterglow Formula" (UAF). Using standard afterglow theories, we derive a set of eight parameters that define afterglow dynamics, and further develop the UAF through a parameterization strategy. By incorporating observational data from 29 GRBs, we formulate a statistical model to determine the probability distributions of these eight parameters. Incorporating the UAF, we simulate the afterglows of 214 GRBs based on their relativistic velocities and electron energies, and compare these simulations with existing observational data. Furthermore, the UAF enables us to recognize specific cosmic structures at large scales by analyzing afterglow behaviors, and we find evidence of an interaction between GRBs and giant arcs of accretion disks orbiting 10-30 $M_{\odot}$ black holes.

The number of split vertices required to convert a non-planar bipartite graph into a planar counterpart has been extensively researched. However, the focus of this study is on the more complex task of identifying a split that allows for a planar embedding, where the number of split vertices is minimal. Building upon Jendrol' and Miller's initial contribution, this paper analyzes the general case (denoted as m-k-Bipartite Splitting) to determine whether a specific bipartite graph can be split into at most k parts with an emphasis on achieving a planar representation. Furthermore, this research introduces enhancements to their algorithm, reducing the time complexity from O(16^k \* n^2) to O(4^k \* n^2) for toting and verifying proposals, and further simplifies the algorithm to O(4^k \* n^2) after introducing a new data structure. Additionally, this study is accompanied by a Trivial Lopsided m-k-Bipartite Splitting variant, targeting a specific subtype of bipartite graphs, for which an efficient solution is proposed with a time complexity of O(n^2).

Deep learning models have achieved a high level of performance in various tasks at the image level, specifically in object detection and segmentation. Nonetheless, accurate prediction of classification probabilities remains an unresolved issue. The goal of this research is to present comprehensive score calibration techniques for deep learning models, focusing on addressing label imbalance. An exhaustive mix of calibration methods and metrics has been examined, and their performance assessed across differing data proportions. Our findings reveal that, although many calibration techniques may seem effective on their own, they can have opposite outcomes when dealing with imbalance. Consequently, a novel straightforward approach, namely data augmentation-based balanced calibration, has been introduced. The proposed method involves calculating the calibration performance on balanced samples achieved through augmentation, rather than utilizing specific loss functions. The benefits of this approach have been demonstrated through undue computational overhead, meaning it's practically feasible for high-dimensional image data. Consequently, it's recommended that future researchers prioritize publishing methods evaluated with balanced data sets.

Researchers have utilized model predictive control to develop efficient gait cycles for bipedal robots under gravity and external influences. This study investigates the benefits of closed-loop feedback on these robots by comparing their performance with and without feedforward control during single support and double support phases. Our findings reveal that closed-loop feedback significantly enhances the robots' stability and efficiency, with notable improvements achieved when feedback is applied to specific joint groups. Incorporating closed-loop feedback allows the robots to maintain balance and optimize energy conservation, with notable reductions in potential energy during gait cycles. In contrast, feedforward control exhibits greater effectiveness in specific situations, particularly when there are larger, more rapid changes in mechanical energy. This research demonstrates the significance of distinguishing between feedforward and feedback controls in complex systems and highlights the need for a comprehensive understanding of closed-loop dynamics to optimize performance across all phases of locomotion.

We demonstrate that for a power series field that has an infinite field at its basis, the power series field equipped with a total residue map does not have computable addition and multiplication functions, provided the basis field is not algebraically closed or has a specific property called infinite differentiation. Conversely, if the basis field is algebraically closed or has a particular property called closed under algebraic extension, we can establish that the power series field with a total residue map is computably stable when equipped with addition, multiplication, and valuation functions. Additionally, if the basis field is algebraically closed or has the property of closed under algebraic extension, we can also show that the power series field with a total residue map is computationally decidable when equipped with addition, multiplication, and valuation functions.

Researchers developed Flush+Reload attacks to counter Memory Disclosure Attacks, but they discovered that these attacks are hinderable. To overcome this limitation, the team created HyperDegrade, which enhances the efficacy of Flush+Reload attacks. HyperDegrade significantly improves time granularity and reduces the necessary traces by a major margin. Additionally, the stakeholders proposed an evaluation method for attack defenses and presented practical implementations of hyperbolized prototypes, yielding impressive results with both standard and optimized libraries. Their findings revealed that anti-Flush+Reload defenses can be vulnerable to hypergradients, enabling the effective exploitation of vulnerabilities even with sophisticated defense systems in place.

The discrepancy remaining in the measurement of the muon's magnetic moment, specifically the $g-2$ anomaly, could be resolved with the introduction of a new particle with a mass anywhere between 40 MeV to over 1 GeV, depending on its complexity. This new particle would interact with the muon and other fundamental particles, potentially influencing other experiments. Even if the $g-2$ anomaly is confirmed, it's unclear whether New Physics would be discovered through other means, such as in searches for rare muon decays or through indirect clues in cosmological and muon experiments. The impact of this new particle on the muon's energy when it is produced as part of the $g-2$ anomaly can result in it having a very short lifetime, making it challenging to detect directly. Nevertheless, it's conceivable that this new particle could also be responsible for other observed phenomena, such as the existence of certain exotic muon states or the generation of neutrino less muon and electron decays. Existing experiments are either on the verge of detecting rare muon decays or have already gathered sufficient data to produce results in the near future. In contrast, information about neutrino less muon and electron decays will only become available in the late 2020s. The new particle's potential influence on the muon's population in future experiments remains unclear and could either enhance or diminish the experiments' sensitivity to their primary research areas. Using precise inclusive measurements of the $B^+ \to J/ψν_ν$ and $B_s \to J/ψν_ν$ decay rates, where $J/ψ$ is a momentum vector, we have developed a new, precise approach to determine the absolute values of the fundamental parameters $m_w$ and $\sin^2θ_w$. This method relies on tree-level decays, taking into account virtual corrections related to $m_w$ and $\sin^2θ_w$, and is unaffected by uncertainties connected to $C_P$ and $C_S$. Taking existing constraints on these uncertainties into account, we find that our results for $m_w$ and $\sin^2θ_w$ are in line with those determined through other methods, and that the former is precise to 0.4% and the latter to 0.3%. Furthermore, our findings yield the top quark mass $m_t$ with a precision of 0.7% and the weak mixing angle $\sin^2θ_w$ with a precision of 0.2% when combined with $m_t$ or $m_w$ determinations from other sources.

By examining the behavior of diagonal crossings in a knotted polymer, researchers have uncovered several interesting properties. A specific diagonal substructure, found within the torus knot of ten crossings, exhibits a peculiar ability to transition between two distinct states while maintaining its topology. This phenomenon is unique among knotted polymers. The study also reveals that this substructure can be reconfigured into a trefoil knot and that its relaxation dynamics are influenced by temperature and chemical environment. The ability to reconfigure this substructure into a trefoil knot was previously unknown. The research is further supported by simulations using a coarse-grained model. These findings are significant because they demonstrate that diagonal substructures within knotted polymers possess functional properties, potentially enabling the development of responsive materials.

Given a finite harmonic morphism $\pi: X \to Y$ between tropical curves and a rational function $f$ on $X$, pulling back $f$ induces a corresponding pull-back $\pi^*(f)$ on the tropicalization level. However, this pull-back may not be well-defined for a rational function $f$ represented by $\frac{g}{h}$, as the pull-back of $\frac{g}{h}$ becomes $\frac{\pi^*(g)}{(\pi^*(h))^\ell}$, with $\ell$ depending on the degree of $\pi$ and the local weights involved. In order to overcome this issue, we redefine pull-back for elements of the semifield of rational functions on $X$ in a way that depends on the local weights associated with $\pi$ and its combinatorial type. In the case where $\pi$ is surjective, this definition aligns with the standard pull-back from the function field perspective. Furthermore, we show that pull-back induces an automorphism of the semifield of rational functions on $X$ and establish connections to harmonic mappings and birational transformations in the tropical world.

We examine how combining specific cocycles affects the development of knot invariants through the construction of a sequence of cocycles in the singular integral operators of the potential theory of harmonic functions. Our potential theory framework is matched to the torus-diagonal operators, providing insight into the related quantum mechanics phenomenon of periodic Schroedinger operators. Our findings suggest that using integrated cocycles results in trefoil-knot-specific invariants, whereas using coccycle integrals produces secure (satellite) knot invariants. We discover that secure knots belong to the class of hyperbolic knots and that our construction related to the torus-centric potential operators resembles the braid representation of the trefoil knot.

We have determined the lowest possible values for the masses of white dwarfs, neutron stars, and the lightest neutrino mass category, given that the universe remains in a stable state. By modeling the structure of stars and considering the effects of neutrino types, we found the minimum mass for a neutral axion-like scalar field-driven stable star to be approximately 0.86 times the solar mass, and this could potentially be achieved by a 10^-3 to 10^-2 eV neutrino of the second type. However, if the universe remains stable without the presence of such a star, we can conclude that the neutrino of the second type must have a minimum mass of about 0.86 times the minimum mass required for a stable star, which would be around 0.5 to 0.7 times the solar mass or, in a scenario without relativistic stars, around 0.4 to 0.6 times the solar mass.

Open-source software for parallel matrix operations is a key enabler of computational linear algebra, and Riemannian manifold algorithms can benefit greatly from its use. In our research, we've created useful extensions to the C++ version of the Eigen library, a popular parallel computing framework, allowing it to efficiently perform matrix operations on various manifolds, including positive definite matrices, Grassmannian, and the special Euclidean group. Our solutions involve developing expressions that are both numerically stable and efficient in terms of computational cost, making extensive use of matrix decompositions and parameterizations. The source code for these extensions has been publicly made available as part of the Eigen project.

In multi-agent learning, coordinating agents can tackle complex tasks together,
with varying levels of difficulty that significantly affect decision-making.
A dynamic environment is introduced in this paper, where agents selectively
choose to work on easy or hard tasks individually, with task difficulty
depending on previous collective achievements.
We study a scenario where an agent wants to decide whether to pursue a challenging
task alone or with others, with the help of a multi-agent deep reinforcement
learning approach.
Our innovative solution involves a system where an agent can choose to be
either an individual leader or a cooperative follower, with different action
spaces and rewards that are disparate by task difficulty.
A unified state-space structure is developed to address the disparate challenges,
enabling the efficient training of a single policy that adapts to varying task
difficulties.
Empirical results show our approach outperforms traditional single-agent solutions
and multi-agent methods, even in the most demanding conditions. The model's ability
to handle diverse challenges is highlighted in thorough tests of its performance
in complex, dynamic environments.

To achieve a higher level of accuracy in theoretical predictions, we are seeing a growing interest in developing new precision strategies. In the context of process-independent uncertainties, our proposed approach provides a comprehensive framework for determining these uncertainties. We have applied our method to calculate the precision required for cross-section calculations at future colliders such as CLIC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, ILC, LHC38, LHC100, and VLHC. We have also developed a new universal factor that can be used to derive the necessary precision for momentum and energy scales, and have determined the factor for each collider. We have further investigated how to optimize the design of these future colliders to achieve the most accurate possible measurements.

This research proves the possibility of violating user privacy in vertical federated learning by uncovering sensitive information about users' categorical attributes and numerical data through a specific attack. We successfully demonstrated the feasibility of these attacks on various federated learning scenarios, including single-party and multi-party settings, utilizing neural networks to achieve substantial accuracy. Our findings show that compared to existing privacy breaches, our attack achieves significantly greater precision and efficiency. We also found that the primary factors contributing to privacy violations are the participation degree, data normalization, and configuration of learning rates. To enhance privacy protection, our study recommends utilizing noise-based protocols and privacy-enhancing architectures. We believe our findings will contribute to the development of more secure vertical federated learning practices.

A recent technique for approximating kernel methods utilizes Random Fourier Features (RFF) which balances efficiency with some preservation of method accuracy. However, by introducing the concept of Pseudo (or Pseudo-Random) RRFeatures (PRFF), we show that a more substantial gain in efficiency can be achieved with either no decline in performance or an improvement, depending on the specific problem. This gain in efficiency enables a dimension reduction equivalent to applying the method directly with an optimal number of Gaussian process components, thus facilitating the approximation of non-parametric Bayesian methods through stochastic variational free energy approximations. We demonstrated the effectiveness of PRFF in relation to RFF across four key signal processing applications, including image denoising, compressed sensing, spectral unmasking, and source separation, and found that using PRFF resulted in either comparable or superior performance to RFF.

Cartesian Decomposition (CD) previously focused on analyzing finite regular group actions and diagonal groups within algebraic geometry. To broaden its applications, the underlying framework should be expanded to include actions and groups in the context of algebraic stacks. This concept is already supported by the generalization of Beilinson-Bernstein localization to affine algebraic stacks. To further this goal, the current work develops the theoretical foundations of CD for actions and diagonal groups within algebraic stacks, with specific examples provided for global quotient stacks and Grassmannians of rank three or higher.

This research paper discloses new findings related to compact, conformally flat hypersurfaces in a higher-dimensional space, specifically within a hypersurface of constant M\"obius scalar curvature in n-dimensional space. The results stated may be applicable to a broader context, potentially contributing to a generalization of the compactness theorem initially proposed by G. Tian and A. Wang. The conditions under which compact, conformally flat hypersurfaces exist relative to M\"obius scalar curvature are defined more precisely, and a lower bound is established for the M\"obius scalar curvature when the hypersurface has a specific, minimal area dimension compared to its dimension in the n-dimensional space. The defined lower bound may be tighter than a previously established lower bound and has a specific, quantitative value. The existence of these compact, conformally flat hypersurfaces is confirmed through a construction process. In addition, the research paper analyzes the stability of these compact, conformally flat hypersurfaces under certain conditions. The findings related to M\"obius scalar curvature provide a basis for further exploration of the compactness theorem in a higher-dimensional space.

Automated cardiac image segmentation has a high potential to streamline clinical workflows, yet its effectiveness heavily relies on the quality of underlying models. Deep learning models, once proven on large, homogeneous datasets, show strong segmentation capabilities. Nevertheless, real-world medical applications frequently involve diverse patient populations, often with uncommon pathologies. This study assesses the robustness of a renowned cardiac image segmentation model when encountered with datasets containing different levels and types of anatomical variations and rare heart pathologies. A multi-center dataset was utilized, comprising 300 3D MRI images from two independent datasets with varying patient demographics and heart conditions. The model's performance was evaluated using a combination of quantitative metrics, including segmentation accuracy, volume estimation, and shape morphology. The results showed a consistent, high performance across two datasets with common heart pathologies, albeit a noticeable decline when encountering a dataset with rare left-ventricular aneurysms. This study's findings highlight the importance of developing robust cardiac image segmentation models capable of handling rare heart variations and multi-center data scenarios, also highlighting the need for larger, more diverse datasets to push the limits of deep learning-based approaches.

This research focuses on developing a computational model to predict the long-term behavior of damaged, heterogeneous materials experiencing gradual degradation. A key characteristic of this approach is the introduction of a non-local mixture theory for damage, which incorporates the concept of a gradient damage function to account for oscillatory changes within the material. To assess the numerical stability of the model, a stability analysis is performed to reveal how small-scale oscillations impact its effectiveness. The findings demonstrate that the non-local approach prevents the development of singularities caused by rapid, short-lived fluctuations, enabling the prediction of stable, long-term behavior. To validate the model, numerical simulations and experimental data analysis are utilized. The results show that the proposed model accurately captures the gradual, large-scale damage progression in materials under both static and dynamic loads, and with various initial conditions.

A novel generalized antenna-switching technique called SWIPT-GET is proposed for energy-efficient data transmission and information reception in split-power transmission scenarios. To analyze this method, an optimization problem is defined that aims to minimize the switching losses in the transmitter by optimizing the antenna selection for data and information transmission while considering the information-theoretic secrecy constraint. To solve this complex minimization problem subject to equality and inequality constraints, a two-step decomposition approach is utilized that involves sequential convex optimization using the Lagrange multiplier method. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations are conducted to demonstrate the performance of the proposed algorithm under various scenario variations, including different network sizes and signal-to-noise ratios. Results show that SWIPT-GET outperforms a conventional phased array antenna in terms of energy efficiency, with a note that an optimal large-scale fading coefficient can be obtained through simple simulation. Additionally, it is shown that increasing the network size or signal-to-noise ratio generally leads to greater gains in energy efficiency.

Recent backbone networks like BNInception, Inception-ResNet and Inception-VRNN have demonstrated exceptional performance in Fast Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN) when implementing a backbone network with repeatable performance. However, these backbones haven't been fully explored for their object detection capabilities, primarily due to their limited public data. We delve into analyzing the performance of these backbones within an FPN architecture through comprehensive experiments, incorporating a diverse range of scale objects in the MJS-30 dataset. Our findings reveal that utilizing a three-times repetition of FPN leads to improved detection accuracy across all scales. We also introduce Contextual Masking (CM) technology to enhance masking precision, combining an unmasked classification result with the masked classification result. Our approach, known as Contextual Masking Network (CMN), delivers superior results compared to the baseline network, outperforming State of the Art (SoA) models on the MJS-30 dataset with an IoU threshold of 0.5.

Given a bivariate distribution where one variable is conditioned on the other, this research develops a statistical method to estimate the distribution of the conditional distribution's tail. This estimation is applied to derive formulas for the expected value and the coefficient of variation of the conditional distribution's tail. The proposed method is demonstrated through explicit calculations for bivariate exponential, lognormal, and normal distributions. The results show the relationship between the original and conditional distributions' tails can be significant, with the latter often being thinner than the former.

Understanding how people comprehend language is a crucial aspect of a machine learning system's language capacity. Comprehending spoken and written language involves making sense of words, phrases, and sentences in various contexts and language variations. There are several key factors that contribute to the difficulty of this task for machines, including the presence of background noise, idioms, and both formal and informal word forms. Gauging a machine's language comprehension ability is similar to assessing a person's language skills, but it requires more complex tests that go beyond simple questions and answers. Unlike humans, machines produce responses in the form of text rather than verbally. The task of evaluating machine language comprehension involves analyzing not just spoken words, but also written communication, including social media and text-based conversations. The ability to learn from examples and fine-tune its performance is a key advantage of modern machine learning architectures in language comprehension. However, a machine's language comprehension ability can be misleading if it performs well on tests but fails to account for noise or only excels in understanding written context. As a result, it is essential to develop tests that help identify not just how well a machine understands language but also its robustness and ability to adapt to various contexts and forms of communication.

Visual dialogue instructions comprise a complex set of orders with no particular order, requiring the understanding of both written and oral instructions and the development of a sequence of actions. Multimodal language models have shown some capacity for sequences of actions, but they still struggle compared to humans, who can accomplish these tasks with ease. The goal of this study is to create more precise models that can provide accurate instructions on how to perform visual dialogue tasks. To achieve this, we present a novel model known as the MultiModal Detailed Follow-Trouble (MM-DET) model, which makes use of detailed troubles and leverages a detailed attention mechanism to enable the generation of more precise instructions. By evaluating the model on two publicly available datasets, we found that it significantly outperforms current approaches and humans have an even higher margin of error.

Inspired by geological phenomena, we develop a non-linear rule to model network breakdown, where the removal of a node generates a subsequent chain reaction. We investigate this process on three diverse networks: an avalanche network, obtained through this non-linear rule applied to a power-law distributed node connectivity, and two standard networks: an original network and one with randomly removed nodes. Surprisingly, in these cases, the degree distribution remains largely unaffected, despite significant changes to the network's structure. However, analyzing the distribution of sizes within the networks reveals a clear pattern, where smaller components are more densely connected and have fewer neighbors than larger components, a phenomenon observable in both the original and fragmented networks. This relationship can be understood through a self-consistency equation, and we identify distinct states corresponding to different size distributions. As expected, larger components play a crucial role in determining the network's conductivity, and we also find that conducting paths may become disconnected during the fragmentation process, significantly impacting the network's overall conductivity.

Holnagel establishes connections between the generalized sextic Freud weights and the x^2 integrable systems, specifically the Toda and Sato systems, using binomial expansion techniques. This involves a modified approach to calculate the corresponding eigenvalues and adjoint eigenvalues. By analyzing the asymptotic behavior of the resulting monodromy matrices, Holnagel shows that the generalized sextic Freud weights correspond to the generalized Airy weights, with the difference lying in a specific quadratic expression. This relationship enables the solution of the Painleve IV equation, and as a consequence, the frequencies, adjoint frequencies, and monodromy matrices for the generalized sextic Freud weights can be determined directly from those of the generalized Airy weights. This relationship also extends to the corresponding Schr\"odinger operators with rational coefficients and periodic potentials, providing solutions to the Stokes line problem for these systems.

A novel type of gravitational wave detector called the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer is presented in this research, which introduces an innovative configuration for enhancing the detector's sensitivity in the high-frequency range. To better understand this new design, the project simulates and compares the performance of a test mass suspended from a truss-like frame in the sloshing-Sagnac setup against a conventional big-totoro-type configuration, incorporating a cross-shaped frame. The findings show that the new design exhibits improved sensor performance in the high-frequency range; however, it suffers from an elevated noise floor due to the increased thermal noise from the truss-like frame. To address this issue, the project proposes a new truss design with a reduced thermal noise frame, made possible by applying a conformal transformation to reframe the problem. This new design features a significantly decreased thermal noise when compared to the original truss-like frame, indicating that further advancements in truss designs could potentially lead to improved sensitivity in the high-frequency range without compromising the noise floor.

As XL-MIMO technology advances with a significantly increased number of antennas, XL-MIMO systems still suffer from poor self-interference and inefficient spectral usage. The underlying orthogonal frequency division multiple access technology remains ill-suited for these complex environments. To address this, a new nonorthogonal variable spacing X-ray computed tomography-based uplink radio access protocol, NOVR-XL RA, is proposed, allowing for simultaneous transmission of multiple signals with distinct spacing patterns, enabling improved spectral efficiency and reduced system complexity. By employing optimized spacing strategies, NOVR-XL RA can separate signals from different access points using computed tomography-based analysis and adaptively adjust the spacing to accommodate changing environmental conditions. To minimize interference and improve detection accuracy, NOVR-XL RA prioritizes access point scheduling based on their spacing adaptability. To optimize NOVR-XL RA, a multiobjective genetic algorithm is employed. With NOVR-XL RA, significant gains in spectral efficiency and system throughput are realized, and overall system complexity is reduced.

A possible theory for the formation of large asteroids and the origins of the Epsilon Aurigae system suggests that substructures in protoplanetary disks may play a key role. These substructures, including the Epsilon Aurigae system and other possible examples, form when a small body detaches from its surrounding disk through the dissimilar rotation rates of the system. In order to investigate this phenomenon, a coupled model of a binary system and its protoplanetary disk was developed. This model took into consideration the effects of the binary's gravitational influence on the disk, as well as the impact of external tides on the system, and used this to analyze the behavior of a protoplanetary disk under the influence of a binary companion. In analyzing the results, particular focus was given to locations where material may become detached due to differing rotation rates. In order to verify the validity of the model, comparisons were made to established limits of gravitational instability. These simulations demonstrated that in systems where the binary's orbit takes approximately 5-20 days to complete, and where the binary's semi-major axis is around 0.1-1 AU, material may become detached at the system's outer boundary, suggesting that future telescopes may have the capability to identify potential candidates for systems like the Epsilon Aurigae system through observations of binary orbits in this range.

A study of nuclear matter properties is conducted using a variety of binding energy functionals, with a particular focus on the BigApple D1R functional. This investigation involves examining the nuclear saturation point, equation of state, and neutron skin depth for a range of neutron-rich nuclei. A detailed comparison is made with experimental data and theoretical predictions from relativistic mean-field models. The research also explores the impact of the functional's effective interaction on one-body density distribution and two-body correlation within the nucleon gas model. Calculated quantities such as binding energies, single-particle energies, and nuclear rotation energies are also determined with the BigApple D1R functional.

Using downfolding and correlated tight-binding models, we investigate the spectral properties of SrMnO$_3$ at the $\Gamma$ point. Our study shows that correlated orbitals contribute significantly to the band structure, influencing it substantially in both the unmagnetized and magnetized states. In the unmagnetized state, our results reveal that the high-energy flat bands and the A1g, Apu/Adu bands arise from correlated orbitals, which are unaffected by spin alignment. Conversely, the median-energy bands exhibit mixed localized and itinerant character and are significantly affected by magnetism, with some becoming filled in the magnetized state. Our findings also highlight that the spin polarization of the itinerant electrons is highly dispersed and lacks clear alignment across the Brillouin zone. These outcomes underscore the importance of incorporating correlated orbitals when analyzing SrMnO$_3$-like compounds, particularly to accurately capture the high-energy and flat bands and to gain a more comprehensive understanding of these compounds' electronic structure.

This research develops a range of Molmer-Sorensen gates with enhanced resistance to errors caused by fluctuations in laser frequencies, particularly useful for protecting complex entanglements in ion chains during quantum simulations. A study on the effects of diode laser fluctuations in the Jaynes-Cummings model highlights the potential for protecting multiple-qubit states. A simple method is presented for calculating the residual entanglement formation even in the presence of frequency errors, leading to the creation of robust Molmer-Sorensen gates via optimization techniques. This approach is applied to design gates capable of withstanding fluctuations up to 10 times more stringent than typical technical limitations, demonstrating the efficacy of this method with experimental validation.

Using a combination of precise experimental measurements and computational modeling,
the structure of the perovskite compound Lanthanum Manganite is investigated.
X-ray and Neutron Scattering show that the material exhibits a distorted cubic
structure, with the manganese and lanthanum ions not evenly distributed within their
respective cells, a phenomenon known as off-centering.
Computational modeling reveals the degree of off-centering is affected by the size
of the filler cations and the material's volume, with an inverse relationship.
In this case, the smaller size of the lanthanum ion relative to the calcium ion
exerts a force causing the manganese ions to shift from their equilibrium positions.
These off-centering effects result in the distortion of the crystal structure,
enabling the material to retain high conductivity even when cooled to very low
temperatures.
These findings demonstrate the significance of off-centering in the physical
properties of perovskites, with potential applications in the development of more
efficient energy storage and conversion technologies.

Researchers have been searching for a compound that combines Dirac electrons and
many-body physics properties, and GaCu$_3$(OH)$_6$Cl$_2$ has been found to fit this bill.
With an unusual structure, this material exhibits unique properties.
It contains two types of crystals: one with Dirac electrons and another with free electrons.
When heated to high temperatures, GaCu$_3$(OH)$_6$Cl$_2$ displays surprising behavior,
losing its magnetic properties and becoming a better conductor of electricity.
Additionally, its crystal structure transforms into a different composition,
and this transformation is influenced by the way the atoms are arranged.
Further study is needed to understand how this compound reacts under pressure,
but it has potential uses in advanced technologies that rely on energy and
magnetic properties, and it also presents an interesting opportunity to study
the interplay between different types of crystals, magnetism, and how the atoms are
arranged, known as the "electron, lattice, and magnetism puzzle".

A new bimodal beta distribution has been proposed, taking a divergent approach to managing data with multiple peaks. Unlike other bimodal distributions, this one segregates the bimodality into distinct, separate components, as opposed to merging them into a single merged mode. We explore the properties of this new distribution, including its bimodal form, moments, and asymptotic behavior. Additionally, we examine the performance of several parametric estimators and provide a detailed analysis of the distribution's characteristics through simulated samples and real-world applications.

The search for heavy neutral leptons at the LHC involves analyzing final states with missing energy and muons or taus. To interpret the results of present and future searches, we need accurate calculations of the branching ratios for these processes. Our study uses the Standard Model Effective Field Theory to find the decay probabilities for heavy neutral leptons decaying into muons, taus, and photons, based on their mass and coupling strengths. To enhance detection sensitivity, we investigate integration time and integrated luminosity in future searches. The most effective approach would be to examine a broader range of heavy neutral lepton masses by utilizing full LHC data at 14 TeV, but this is not feasible with current resources. However, if we limit the search to recently discovered neutral particles, we can narrow the effective field theory parameter space quite significantly.

We examine the unidirectional operation of a Sagnac interferometer by investigating the effects of longitudinal Doppler shift and laser absorption on counter-propagating beams. Our analysis reveals a previously unconsidered impact of the longitudinal Doppler shift, along with the action of laser absorption, on the balance of counter-propagating beams within the Sagnac circuit. As a result, the estimated velocity and frequency shift become distorted, comprising inaccurate information. To overcome this limitation, we propose a method to isolate the velocity shift by operating the Sagnac interferometer in a bidirectional manner, using the difference between outgoing and incoming spectra. This approach enables precise measurement of the frequency shift and velocity shift, thus providing unbiased estimates.

We prove that a complex, non-algebraic variety of the type defined by nilfibre structures contains no dense orbits under the action of a certain subgroup, specifically the one generated by the standard set of holomorphic vector fields. This is accompanied by a counterexample featuring a real, defined nilfibre variety, demonstrating that such varieties can exhibit dense orbits within a subgroup. Additionally, we establish the equivalence between complex, defined nilfibre varieties and those with minimal, minimal-generated orbits, providing a key insight into our primary conclusion.

The integration of $N$-gram models and neural language models has been shown to lead to significant advancements in machine learning tasks like machine translation, summarization, and speech recognition. This approach, where a neural model guides an $N$-gram model to avoid rare words, can result in a balance between accuracy and fluency. Our research builds upon this concept, introducing a method to dynamically select the order of the $N$-gram model based on the neural model's classification of words as frequent or rare. This proposed technique, involving the dynamic selection of $N$-gram models, was tested on a translation task using the WMT'14 English-to-German dataset and demonstrated an enhanced performance, achieving a higher BLEU score than both the system it was compared to and the baseline.

Laurent polynomials provide an equivalent representation of tropical polynomials and their mutation behavior aligns with the geometric characteristics of Fano varieties in higher dimensions. By establishing connections between these characteristics and big line bundles, the study aims to build a bridge between the geometric and combinatorial aspects of Fano varieties. To achieve this, the concept of closed convex bodies, which encompasses moment polytopes, is introduced and its properties explored. The proof of convexity for closed bodies associated with closed cones involves the application of persistence of convex bodies to simplify complex geometric characteristics. Furthermore, the proof of convexity for bodies related to line bundles involves the introduction of a new measure related to the volume of convex bodies. By establishing the convexity of these bodies, the study provides a foundation for further exploration of the properties of line bundles and combinatorial characteristics.

Recently, research on the disentangled representation of 3D faces has focused primarily on separating expressional variations from identity and pose. Nevertheless, the task remains complex due to the closely linked nature of facial angles which make tasks like isolated expression synthesis extremely difficult. To tackle this issue, we propose the Self-aligned Dual face Regression Network (SADRNet) which uses a dual-regression framework to create a 3D face from both pose-dependent and pose-independent factors. In this model, the pose-independent factor is used to generate the face's overall structure while the pose-dependent factor is employed to adjust the face's geometry to match desired angles. To achieve this, we utilize a dual-regression framework in which the pose-dependent factor is estimated by aligning the generated face with the target face under varying rotations. Through extensive experiments on the widely-used ABLF and Expressives datasets, our SADRNet showcases remarkable performance in disentangling rotations and expressions. Moreover, our network exhibits superior performance in isolated expression synthesis and scene-specific face reconstruction compared to current state-of-the-art methods. All code and models are available at: https://github.com/TrinhVu/SADRNet.

Researchers have found that certain systems exhibiting gapped fracton orders may still possess charge density and display unique mobility properties. This work examines the effects of a finite charge density on the mobility of fractons within a system characterized by interacting bosons in optical lattances. The study shows that the interplay between different mobility modes and the formation of a finite charge density lead to the degradation of fracton mobility, with the impact varying depending on the strength of the interaction between sublattices. The findings suggest that stronger interactions cause the mobility of individual sublattices to dominate, while weaker interactions result in the prevalence of fracton mobility due to the formation of a finite charge density that facilitates communication between sublattices. The work also predicts the possibility of observing fracton-like behavior at the edge states in such systems when the drive strength exceeds a certain threshold, demonstrating an intriguing connection between bulk and boundary properties. The potential for realizing robust zero-energies in these systems is an exciting outcome of this investigation.

A study has been conducted to examine the effects of the scalar power spectrum on the Bardeen potential in the late stages of inflation and during the subsequent period of rapid expansion known as the 'late inflation' or 'extended inflation' period. It has been observed that in these scenarios, large negative values of the Bardeen potential develop, influencing the formation of primordial black holes and modifying the characteristics of the cosmological background. A relationship between the scalar power spectrum and the Bardeen potential was identified through a perturbative analysis in the context of a two-field model representing the 'waterfall' scenario. The findings also illustrate the potential for the scalar power spectrum to be affected by the inflationary dynamics in multi-field scenarios.

Research into the structure of ordered trees has been limited by a lack of random ordered trees for reference. To address this, standard ordered trees were introduced and their properties studied. Now, with the ability to analyze ordered trees, a new investigation considers the number of deepest nodes in standard ordered trees. In contrast, a separate line of research involving the placement of distinct objects into ascending order identifies a significantly lower average number of deepest nodes. To bridge this gap, new insights are gained through the construction of marked ordered trees, showing that the majority of standard ordered trees have multiple deepest nodes. Additionally, results are derived to further characterize the structure of standard ordered trees, including the distribution of the number of deepest nodes, node heights, and the height of the tree. These new findings provide a complete picture of standard ordered trees, clarifying previous misconceptions and shedding light on the underlying structure.

To facilitate accurate optical character recognition, a spin-off benefit is derived from a more sophisticated spell checking algorithm applied to incorrect character readings. This study scrutinizes the performance of the spell checking algorithm, initially developed for North American English, when utilized on data from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds encountered in election voting. A significant improvement from a Levenshtein distance-based method to one employing Levenshtein distances in both directions is observed, yielding better results. Furthermore, the algorithm's effectiveness is examined in relation to various misreads, including those affecting a single character, adding one character, or deleting one character.

In the context of learning linear models, where both the data dimensions are infinite and the model is over-parameterized, neural tangent skews are used as an efficient way to build a linear approximation of the model. This technique is particularly challenging to extend to time-dependent variables due to the infinite data dimensions and the need for a compact parameterization.
