A comprehensive historical analysis of the subject has been long overdue, and we believe it high time to illuminate this aspect of XAI. In this survey, we traverse through the evolutionary milestones of neural networks, from the early work of McCulloch and Pitts to the emergence of modern neural languages models. Along the journey, we explore the influential applications and key contributors to the field, highlighting the pressing issues that remain to be addressed in this realm. We hope this excursion through the past will not only provide a sense of direction for the current research but also inspire future generations to build upon this foundation and push the boundaries of neural networks.

We conducted an in-depth analysis of the star KIC 9267654, involving a detailed examination of its internal rotation pattern. This involved measuring the line broadening in multiple spectral ranges, as well as the shift of lines formed at different latitudes, and comparing them with theoretical predictions based on stellar structure. Our calculations show that KIC 9267654's rotation may be unique, with a slow axial rotation and faster latitudinal variation, at odds with standard mixing theories. It's also noteworthy that this star exhibits similar characteristics to the Empress CS, with regards to its internal rotation. Further investigation into KIC 9267654's past may provide insight into the recent changes observed in this star, as well as the star's future evolution.

The rapid dissemination of news through social platforms in recent years has led to the rapid spread of false information, causing concern and difficulty in managing its impact. The task of identifying false information, or fake detection, has become increasingly vital in ensuring the quality of online information. Although the advancement of deep learning and massive labeled data has improved detection performance, obtaining large amounts of labeled data remains a significant challenge. To address this issue, a novel approach called MetaFEND was proposed, leveraging the principles of meta-learning to develop a flexible model capable of detecting false information on a large scale. By utilizing a multi-task architecture and introducing a novel task-adapter module based on a flexible attention mechanism, MetaFEND effectively reduces the need for extensive labeled data. The proposed approach was evaluated on the Facebook News False Information Detection Dataset and outperformed existing models, demonstrating the efficacy of meta-learning in detecting false information.

We examine a one-dimensional transport equation periodic in the x-direction and time, with a nonlocal flux function and no dissipative elements, applied to initial conditions that are smooth, periodic in x, and specifically odd in the variable y. The existence and uniqueness of the solution can be confirmed by applying the semiflow to the given initial conditions within its invariant space. Furthermore, we observe that the solution exhibits periodic behavior in both x and y variables at all times, with a periodicity that aligns with the given parameters. In the case where the nonlocal flux exhibits a singular relationship with the distance from the origin, the solution develops an oscillatory pattern as time progresses, characterized by increasing frequency and amplitude. This conclusion can be reached by applying the singular perturbation theory.

This paper compares the stationary average of absolute time ages (AoI) in discrete and continuous time systems with similar update characteristics. We establish a new expression for the stationary AoI distribution in discrete time systems, showing it follows a key distribution (KD) shape, and provide a specific example to demonstrate this outcome. A previous study by our research group already derived the stationary AoI expression in continuous time systems. Our findings reveal that discrete and continuous time systems with the same update characteristics have distinct stationary AoI distribution shapes, highlighting the limitations of applying continuous time models to discrete time systems. These findings have implications for the development of age-optimal control policies, particularly highlighting the need for different approaches in discrete and continuous time settings.

Drinfeld's theory of twists for automorphisms of algebraic groups and their implementation in the context of representation theory, particularly for affine algebraic groups, have been found to yield valuable insights and results. This paper delves into the characteristics of Drinfeld twists that remain invariant under the algebraic group's adjoint action, documenting both set-theoretic and quadratic-deformed analogues of such invariant twists. Furthermore, it explores the relationship between these invariant twists and Deligne-Lusztig theory, establishing a connection that holds in both the classical and deformed settings.

This research focuses on the theoretical development of a quaternary Golay complementary array pair in $t$ dimensions, and we're particularly examining its applicability in four-dimensional space. A necessary condition for such a pair to exist in four dimensions requires that a corresponding binary Golay complementary array pair also exists in $t$ dimensions. We've previously demonstrated the feasibility of quaternary GACPs in one, two, and three dimensions, but this research goes further to explicitly confirm the necessary condition for a quaternary GACP to exist in four-dimensional space, and in doing so, we explicitly establish the parameters required for a quaternary GACP to be feasible in four-dimensional space.

We investigate how the placement of 29Si and 31V dopants affects the Heisenberg spin exchange interaction in a silicon crystal lattice. Using a combination of NMR and optical techniques on isotopically enriched samples containing a single pair of exchange-coupled spins, we directly measure the strength of this interaction for various dopant positions, including substitutional and interstitial sites, as well as different crystallographic directions. Our findings reveal a significant influence of the dopants' location on the exchange interaction, with a particular sensitivity to their spatial arrangement. When both spins occupy the same sublattice, the interaction becomes either very strong or very weak, depending on their relative orientation, while a significant variation in the exchange coupling occurs when they are positioned on different sublattances, leading to a considerable adjustment of the exchange interaction when placed interstitially. These results provide a thorough understanding of the exchange interaction and its complex dependence on the dopants' position within the silicon lattice.

The underlying structure of a complex system can be challenging to dissect due to its ever-changing nature and the limited availability of its specifications. Complex systems, such as electrical grids and transportation networks, consist of multiple interacting components that shape their behavior and dynamics. When confronted with a new system and limited information about its structure, we can leverage observations from the time series data it generates to inform its underlying structure through probabilistic inference. This paper introduces a novel approach, novel approach included in this paper, which employs a hybrid model combining multi-task grid learning and variational autoencoders to extract the system's structural features from its time series observations. Showcasing the effectiveness of this method on multiple testing scenarios using artificial and real-world data, we find that it outperforms alternative methods and significantly improves the accuracy of structural feature recovery by up to 75%. Furthermore, this approach successfully applies to varying operational conditions and system sizes.

This talk will explore how graded polynomial rings are employed to examine partitions within stable homotopy theory, highlighting their significance and interpreting the results through the lens of partition diagrams.

Automated region-of-interest (ROI) segmentation in medical imaging has seen significant advancements, primarily through the use of deep learning convolutionsal neural networks, which have demonstrated a high capacity for complex pattern recognition. Despite such progress, the time it takes to train these networks remains a significant concern for many real-world medical applications. In an effort to address this issue, this study seeks to investigate the potential benefits of using a highly efficient network known as CoNet, which was initially designed for computing compact CNNs through a method called group-wise convolution. By evaluating CoNet in various scenarios involving ROI segmentation, the researchers aim to assess its performance against more conventional network structures using techniques such as batch normalization and leaky ReLU activation functions. According to the findings presented, the researchers suggest that using adaptations of both batch normalization and leaky ReLU along with elements of CoNet, which incorporates a method called weighted grouping, leads to improved results while also reducing training time and the memory required for ROI segmentation tasks. In particular, this study shows that by leveraging these adaptations and weighted grouping, the modified network produces a more compact representation with fewer parameters than the baseline, resulting in significant reductions in both training time and the required memory for two key ROI segmentation tasks.

In this context, we investigate how strong quantum nonlocality can be demonstrated in multipartite settings by showing that a limited set of product states, specifically unextendible product bases, are sufficient to span the quantum states exhibiting strong nonlocality when applied to certain types of qudits (d-dimensional systems). We first establish the principle that any set of product states containing a certain number of local bases can be re-basis-transformed into a set of local product states representing strong nonlocality, and we determine the minimum number of local product states required to achieve this. We further examine the applicability of this principle to various multipartite settings involving qudits of different dimensions and discuss the relevant concepts of extended product bases and their connection to strong nonlocality. By applying this framework, we identify and demonstrate strong nonlocality in multiple scenarios, including a four-dimensional scenario with only three local product bases.

To facilitate expansive astrobiochemical surveys in collaborative environments between humans and robots, we need to ensure that robotic paths are both secure and energy-efficient. A optimization technique utilizing a hybrid model that combines reconfigurable ring networks and sub-modular function optimization is introduced in this paper to achieve this goal. This method was successfully tested on a hypothetical scenario involving survey missions around Earth, and the results showed significant improvements in solving the co-flight planning problem compared to existing solutions. The improved performance was found to include enhanced efficiency and accuracy in solving larger-scale problems. Additionally, this method displayed the ability to generate more precise solutions in a shorter amount of time. All code related to this research is openly accessible on GitHub.

The second edition of the GP 2019 conference introduced a new data structure called BigArray, which led to a significant enhancement in graph program performance and enabled the flexible management of large-scale array data. In response, multiple researchers submitted innovative ideas to further optimize BigArray performance, expand its applications within graph programs, and clarify its theoretical underpinnings. As a result, the conference organizers decided to extend the submission deadline for the GP 2020 special issue by three months to allow more time for reviewers to thoroughly assess these contributions. Ultimately, the issue featured eight high-quality submissions, each meticulously reviewed by renowned experts in the GP field. The resulting set of 11 articles presents an exhaustive exploration of BigArray's optimized implementations, its innovative use cases within graph programs, and in-depth analyses of BigArray's theoretical properties. The researched topics include non-blocking parallel algorithms for BigArray operations, a recursive approach for creating BigArray, an evaluation of functional programming with BigArray in Java, and several groundbreaking applications of BigArray in science and engineering, encompassing numerical computations, solver implementations, and computational biology applications.

A single framework is introduced for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction on single and multi-camera settings. This approach uses cross-camera consistency to extract unsupervised features and is applied to various supervised tasks after receiving labeled training data. Our method stands out from other supervised feature extraction techniques that only consider pairwise comparisons. Instead, our proposed framework leverages cross-camera relations to inform the feature learning process, leading to more relevant and discriminative features. This is supported by quantitative results showing our approach yields superior performance in supervised tasks compared to methods that use labeled data alone.

We have developed an infinite family of periodic graphs of minimal radius for each $d \ge 3$, along with a second infinite family of periodic graphs whose automorphism group is abelian for each $d \ge 4$. Both of these new families surpass previous records for graph diameter among the periodic category.

The Group Lasso algorithm, a powerful tool for variable selection, can be applied to both continuous and categorical data variables. This technique has been successfully integrated into Random Forest and Support Vector Machines to improve model performance and reduce dimensions. To facilitate easy implementation of the Group Lasso algorithm for categorical variables, the R package 'grouplasso' is provided, allowing users to utilize the least absolute selection and correction and group Lasso algorithms via the CVXOPT and GLOW library. To enhance performance, the package includes options for variable clustering and relaxation. To evaluate the package's effectiveness, the 'grouplasso' package is applied to default and clinical datasets to demonstrate its variable selection capabilities.

This investigation compares pre-trained models that use knowledge graph triples to those using traditional text-based data for question-answering tasks. Our assessments involve multiple models, questions, and knowledge graphs, testing their performance in both full and zero-shot scenarios. Our key findings reveal that pre-trained models on knowledge graphs significantly outperform baseline models and consistently excel in question-answering performance across various models and datasets. Moreover, our experiments show that high-performance models utilizing knowledge graphs excel in question-answering tasks, even in zero-shot scenarios, demonstrating a capacity for answering complex questions devoid of explicit support.

This article examines how classical partial differential equation (PDE) models are linked to nonlocal diffusion equations with decreasing interaction kernels, with a focus on the scenario where the kernel exhibits near-local behavior and brief memory effects are present. We establish a relationship between these nonlocal equations and their corresponding classical PDE models, leveraging this connection to develop a new numerical approach for nonlocal equations. Our novel strategy adapts classical local solvers, incorporating the decreasing kernel into the equations to achieve superior precision and convergence rates comparable to those of classical methods. We demonstrate the success of this approach through numerical experiments and an in-depth analysis of the method's performance.

We are tackling the challenge of creating seamless panoramic images using portable devices with internal sensors. Our key innovation is a non-rigid synthesis technique that allows for the alignment of images captured by Inertial Measurement Units. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in real-world applications, and our work lays the groundwork for advanced panoramic capture techniques that could revolutionize mobile photography.

We establish a clear and comprehensive framework for analyzing degenerate Eisenstein series under specific, general local settings. Our framework specifically examines Weyl group cosets and related orbital integrals. By applying this framework, we derive explicit formulae for degenerate Eisenstein series, drawing parallels with earlier findings by H. Jacquet and C. J. Bushnell and P. J. Kilburn. Our approach also extends the scope of earlier results by H. Jacquet and C. J. Bushnell and P. J. Kilburn, capturing a broader class of Eisenstein series.

The significant rise in complex computational models demands a higher level of
analysis to ensure the understanding of modeled processes and the detection of
errors, particularly in critical applications like Parkinson's Disease research.
Developing a code analysis tool for model verification, we created a prototype
using a model of the striatal reward system, which includes LFP data from rat
experiments and simulated neural networks. We successfully utilized this tool to
identify an error in the code that affects the model's accuracy. The code and tool
are available online, and we invite researchers to use them for their own research
and verify models for diseases like Parkinson's, movement disorders, and neurodegenerative diseases.

This research presents a novel approach to creating high-quality renders of the connections between lines that intersect at an angle. Unlike standard techniques which can produce uneven results for concave intersections, the proposed method uses a geometric analysis to break the junction down into more manageable parts, ensuring a smooth and consistent appearance across all types of intersections. A key benefit of this approach is its ability to be optimized for parallel processing, making it particularly suited for use in high-performance rendering environments. A key component of the proposed algorithm is its use of a step-wise method to break down the line connection, ensuring that the rendered output accurately represents the original input. This approach has significant implications, as it means that any distortions introduced during the rendering process can be minimized, resulting in a more faithful representation of the original data. A key aspect of the proposed algorithm is its alignment with modern rendering pipelines, and we demonstrate this by applying it to a range of use cases, including scientific visualizations and 3D maps.

Recent discoveries of AGN-driven outflows, which can affect galaxy mergers by inhibiting star formation and the growth of supermassive black holes, have shifted the focus from mergers to the role of outflows in the galaxies' co-evolution. These outflows are powered by the energy released from the conversion of kinetic energy into thermal energy during the AGN's radiative processes, which in turn is influenced by the availability of gas for outflowing and being absorbed by the AGN. In this study, we utilize gas-progressive outflows driven by radiative AGN to model outflows that can weaken during collisions, assuming outflows prioritize gas with the lowest binding force. Our simulations indicate outflows can steer minor mergers with minimal mass ratios and avoid collisions with massive satellites, while also preventing outflows from being disrupted during encounters. Additionally, our findings show outflows can cause rings of obstructed star formation around galaxies that experience near-head-on collisions, a phenomenon observable in recent studies. This implies outflows have the capability to significantly impact galaxy mergers and the co-evolution of galaxies and supermassive black holes, potentially leading to reduced major mergers and a slower growth of supermassive black holes throughout the universe.

This study introduces a novel class of rational piecewise polynomial functions in the context of radial basis function approximation, ensuring these functions retain both convexity and monotonicity properties. Building upon the concept of quasi-interpolation, a corresponding method is developed to achieve optimal approximation, and the associated error is analyzed. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms the conventional method based on interpolation. A specific implementation of the new function, comprising a combination of alignable multiquadric and linear components, is examined numerically to showcase its efficiency and accuracy.

Data augmentation techniques like Delaunay Triangulation and super pixel limiting masks are used in this research to improve the application of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) in agricultural image classification, specifically for identifying the maturity stage of tomatoes. A CBS (Combined Board Strategy) data augmentation method was developed and incorporated into a CNN model to enhance its performance. The evaluation of the method's effectiveness involved conducting 9 repeat experiments for each of 4 data augmentation techniques at different image resolution levels (64x64, 128x128, 256x256). The results showed that the CBS method yielded the highest accuracy rates of 94.17%, 97.58%, and 96.58% for mature tomato detection at 64x64, 128x128, and 256x256 image resolutions, respectively. These findings suggest that the CBS method can effectively improve the accuracy of CNN models in identifying tomato maturity stages across various image resolutions.

A recent deep learning method known as the Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) has been highly effective in the time-frequency domain for speech enhancement, transforming the spectrogram of noisy speech into that of clean speech. This network comprises two distinct pathways: one using a convoluted neural network and the other using a recurrent neural network, which feed their outputs into a common summing point and are combined to produce the final spectrogram. As a result, DPCRN generates speech spectra with significant improvements, but its underlying reasoning has not been fully understood. To further refine DPCRN, it is essential to analyze its components separately and explore alternative architectures. Consequently, the next stage of development for DPCRN involves reviewing its current implementations, discussing associated challenges and potential solutions, and examining innovative techniques for post-processing the derived spectrograms to restore clean speech.

A fascinating feature of galaxies in the late stages of assembly is the turn-around phase. Galaxies during this phase exhibit unique characteristics that allow for a direct connection between their mass and spatial configuration. Turn-around phases provide an opportunity to investigate the matter distribution and galaxy formation processes within a specific, well-defined mass range. By examining the matter distribution in turn-around phases, we can gain insights into the structure of galaxies forming from dark matter. A galaxy-to-galaxy variation in the turn-around radii ratios was previously observed and modeled using a simplified approach that takes into consideration the interplay between dark matter, gas, and stars. Our study introduces a statistical analysis to account for variations in a way that respects the constraints of dark matter behavior as outlined in the CHAMcock model. By incorporating uncertainty in the radii ratios, we can break down the uncertainty in mass estimates. A statistical comparison with passive spectroscopy and star formation observations will help paint a complete picture of galaxy formation during the turn-around phase. Additionally, we will investigate the possibility of using turn-around phases as cosmological probes by analyzing the density profiles of multiple galaxies. A statistical analysis of the mass function of galaxies during the turn-around phase also shows significant structure at a given mass range, indicating that the model can effectively capture the formation process of galaxies during this phase. However, the model falls short in accounting for the mass function of galaxies at the turn-around phase due to an artificial margin, which could be an indication of a threshold effect in the

A simple two-fluid model is used to analyze the thermal plumes in Rayleigh-Bénard convection, and it leads to a heat flux ratio that follows a $1/3$ power law in relation to the Prandtl number. By introducing a variable viscosity that is proportional to the square of the temperature difference, the model reveals a distinct regime where the heat flux becomes exponentially dependent on the square of the Rayleigh number, consistent with recent empirical findings.

When a cavity is surrounded by a large number of identical, randomly behaving atoms, and only one special atom with minimal fluctuation has a correlation with the cavity, this scenario models a situation effectively. It illustrates the limitations of entanglement between different atoms when the cavity is linked to a single, unconnected atom. This model can help us understand the challenges of achieving multipartite entanglement in this system. When the cavity is isolated from the environment and there is no photon loss, applying a series of resonant laser pulses can entangle any number of atoms with the cavity. However, due to photon loss, this complex entanglement may transform into a higher-angle-resonance when more atoms are included, ultimately leading to a change in the angle of resonance as the number of atoms increases. This model can also cover other types of atom-cavity interactions where the resonance occurs at an angle other than 90 degrees. In such cases, higher-angle resonances may emerge when more atoms are included, allowing for the potential to create complex entanglements in this system.
Between 2016 and 2021, the CMS detector at the LHC underwent significant upgrades to its silicon pixel detector, which showcased enhanced performance and operational stability during that period.

Researchers have been attempting to identify the glueball spectrum through the study of isotropic two-dimensional QCD using Monte Carlo methods at various temperatures. This study uses a novel approach to analyze the glueball spectrum by examining the correlation between the SU(2) plaquette and the temperature. The results show a clear peak in the second derivative of the plaquette with respect to the temperature at approximately 0.49 times the deconfinement temperature, indicating the presence of an excited state. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the glueball mass can be extracted from the plaquette's temperature dependence in the confined phase and estimates the mass of the first excited state to be approximately twice the mass of the ground state. The findings also support previous studies indicating that the glueball mass is independent of the temperature and lies within the range of 0.42 to 0.53 times the deconfinement temperature.

In addressing the challenge of detecting hate speech and bullying in social media, it's essential to develop efficient methods for identifying and classifying toxic and pleasant content. This task is complicated by the limited amount of annotated data available for each topic. To tackle this, we propose a new approach that employs a LSTM model to classify the sentiment of individual tweets and a cluster-based approach to classify the sentiment of articles based on their content clusters. To enhance the model's performance, we utilize both supervised and unsupervised learning techniques to create more effective features. In evaluating our method on Twitter data, we demonstrate that our approach yields superior results compared to conventional methods, despite being computationally composable. The proposed technique achieves superior performance, with a micro-F1 score of 93.5, outperforming the baseline by a margin of 11.5 points. Furthermore, our model exhibits superior performance to the baseline in the context of Twitter data, surpassing the baseline by a substantial margin of 11.5 points.

A new Holographic Dark Energy model is presented, where the non-linear Yang-Mills charge is used to determine the cosmological constant in a charged AdS$_4$ black hole. The relationship between the non-linear charge and the event horizon radius in five-dimensional linear Yang-Mills theory is examined, and it is found that the non-linear charge raises the event horizon, increases the shadow radius, and alters the thermal profile of the black hole. The proposed HDE model is consistent with a variety of astronomical observations, including the rate of the universe's expansion, the distance to type Ia supernovae, and the clustering of galaxy distributions. The model also predicts a value for the Hubble constant that is in line with the results of recent astronomical observations. The proposed HDE model leads to a variation in the growth rate of galaxy distributions, and it is observable in the large-scale structure of the universe.

The study explores the connection between nonclassical behavior and optical tomogram features in the context of Mach-Zehnder interferometry involving coherent states. The effects of entanglement and dichotomous classical noise on optical tomograms are examined, and their nonclassical characteristics analyzed using the Glauber-Sudarshan P-representation. The findings show that certain classical noise patterns can mimic the effects of entanglement, suggesting that noise type may not be unambiguously determined from optical tomograms alone. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the Mach-Zehnder interferometer can distinguish between entanglement and classical noise, and proposes using the von Neumann entropy as a metric to measure such nonclassical behavior.

The success of data-driven dialogue systems heavily relies on their ability to accurately follow user instructions. This capability is often assessed through human-conversational tests, which provide a reliable evaluation of a system's performance. To enhance the effectiveness of this evaluation, the instruction guidelines should be clearly defined to enable other researchers to reproduce the results. In the context of the NIcal mixed-domain dialogue dataset, the original instructions were originally intended for a single-domain system, but it is now possible to apply these instructions to a broader range of environments. This extended dataset includes additional datasets for the news and weather domains and incorporates a revised set of role specifications that are consistent with the original guidelines. A human-conversational evaluation of the NICAL mixed-domain dialogue dataset involved multiple systems, each designed to operate across four domains, and demonstrated a notable gap of over 100 ASPA scores in terms of mean ASPA.

This research develops an economic model of disease management for strawberries, incorporating the effects of disease on plant mortality and productivity, as well as the impact of control methods on disease spread and management costs. We applied mathematical techniques to analyze the model, focusing on its equilibrium points to understand the interplay between disease prevalence, plant density, and management decisions. Computer simulations were used to examine how different disease control methods affect the long-term outcome in scenarios representative of California's strawberry industry practices. We found that, in scenarios with moderate to high disease pressure, integrated pest management can lead to increased profits and yields, but this may not always be the case in scenarios with low disease pressure. We also found that, in response to the presence of the disease, the model prefers thinner spacings and more frequent harvests, along with a greater reliance on the more expensive chemical control as the disease spreads. However, these outcomes can vary depending on the specific conditions and technological parameters. The model provides valuable insights into the complex relationships involved in strawberry disease management, although its applicability is limited to above-ground diseases like powdery mildew. The development of this model involved a review of the existing literature on the economics of disease management, the theoretical analysis of the model, and a discussion of its policy implications.

Immersive videos, being complex and dynamic, pose a significant challenge to viewport prediction models. A crucial aspect that can enhance the prediction accuracy involves video subtitles, which provide verbal descriptions of the visual content and are often overlooked. In this research, we introduce a novel approach that leverages subtitles and multi-task learning to improve viewport prediction performance. Unlike traditional approaches that focus solely on visual features, our method incorporates subtitle embeddings to enhance the representation of video information. We developed two versions of this approach, incorporating either single-task learning with the multi-task learning framework or dual-task learning with shared embeddings, and applied them to a dataset with both subtitle and audio components. Compared to baseline models, our proposed methods exhibited better prediction accuracy, with dual-task learning outperforming single-task learning. This research demonstrates the significance of video subtitles in viewport prediction and provides a groundwork for future studies.

Researchers seek to utilize tensor networks to efficiently compute thermal states and time-evolved dynamics by breaking down complex many-body systems into more manageable, local units. A promising approach involves using single-system objects, such as linear clusters or spin chains, to build highly entangled tensors that capture the spirit of thermal states and time evolution. However, it is unclear how these approximations' bond dimension requirements change relative to system size in the constructed combined objects. This study addresses this inquiry by developing two types of tensor networks - Multi-Sys PEPO and DetPEPO - that consist of multiple independent systems with a single entanglement bond, allowing us to precisely control the bond dimension's system-size dependence. Our findings indicate that the entanglement bond's rank must roughly double with each additional spin in a one-dimensional chain to properly approximate its thermal state and time-evolved dynamics. Notably, our study reveals that the double-scaling phenomenon's rate is insensitive to the interaction strength or type. Instead, it is governed by the two-body operator's rank, specifically whether it spans a space of minimal or half-minimal rank. As a result, systems with rank-deficient interactions, such as the Heisenberg model, exhibit faster-growing bond dimension needs than those with full-rank interactions, such as the XXZ model.

This lecture will outline the basic components of two analytical strategies, 
Taylor-based analysis and canonical surfaces, and demonstrate their combined 
application to understand the relationships between wave maps, solitons, and 
decoupling estimates.

This paper introduces the anisotropic capacity of Tuza-Kolesnik and Strichartz as a specific case of the $p$-norm capacity, and demonstrates its connection to established volumetric inequalities, including the Poincar\'{e} inequality and the Kato inequality. The anisotropic capacity of Tuza-Kolesnik and Strichartz can be viewed as the $p$-norm capacity with $p = \frac{N}{N-1}$, where $N$ represents the dimension of the space. We establish the relationship between this capacity and the $L^p$ norm, demonstrating that it serves as an equivalent norm for $p \in (1, \infty)$. We then employ this equivalence to prove the boundedness of the anisotropic Riesz transforms and the anisotropic Davis-Journ\'{e} operators within the corresponding Lorentz spaces. These results may be regarded as an extension of the findings introduced by Tuza-Kolesnik and Strichartz.

Researchers participating in the Space Accelerometer experiment utilized an array of six to eight phone-based accelerometers mounted on a randomly moving object to test an aspect of the Mach-Einstein equivalence principle. These accelerometers were then compared to a highly sensitive, custom-built reference accelerometer in a suborbital flight to measure the effects of gravitational acceleration on acceleration measurements, specifically in microgravity and during gravitational descent. However, it was discovered that the data contained glitches, which are brief spikes resulting from the random movement of the object and environmental interference. These glitches needed to be filtered out to produce reliable results. In microgravity, the data showed a glitch-driven bias of 0.5 nanogals, but this was minimized through data processing techniques to an acceptable level for the test requirements. The most significant outcome was the determination of a glitch-induced reference system bias of 0.2 nanogals during gravitational descent. This outcome was consistent with pre-flight predictions and highlighted the importance of considering the effects of real-world movement on sensor readings.

Certain active dimers exhibit unique spinning motions, resembling how a wheel turns in vehicles, and this comparison can be made for varicose active dimers that transition between parallel and anti-parallel states. Researchers have previously successfuly applied temperature gradients to power these dimers, but now they also want to investigate the possibility of using chemical gradients to drive their spinning. Using a model based on the Michaelis-Menten mechanism, they analyze the effectiveness of chemical gradients in varicose active dimers with different tightness levels. The results show that in highly stiff dimers, chemical gradients can still efficiently generate spinning motion, despite reducing the dimensionless driving force to a minimum. In contrast, less stiff dimers demonstrate an interesting reversal, where chemical gradients actually cause the dimers to move in the opposite direction, effectively creating a "reverse gear" effect. This finding could lead to the development of more complex dynamical behaviors in macroscopic devices inspired by these dimers.

We examine the k-strong shortest path union cover problem, which involves finding the fewest number of sets required to cover all nodes in a graph, where each set represents the shortest paths connecting specific node pairs. These sets must be part of a subgraph that has k-strong connections, meaning it can reach all nodes with up to k edge hops. We show that solving this problem is computationally complex (NP-hard) and offer two alternative solutions that cover all nodes with a higher number of strong connections (k+1 and k+2 respectively). We also investigate the relationship between the number of sets and the strength of connections it provides (k) and propose a heuristic method for improving results.

A systematic approach has been developed to account for systematic errors in functions of hadrons, utilizing renormalon theory. This methodology has been applied to derive the uncertainty in the $x$-dependent gluon distribution, specifically for its contribution to the jet production in deep inelastic scattering. The resulting uncertainty, once incorporated into a corresponding JIMWY function, shows a significant increase in the uncertainty in jet structure functions when compared to conventional perturbative QCD calculations. Incorporating this uncertainty into corresponding cross-sections for deep inelastic scattering shows a notable impact on predictions, particularly for small $x$ and with low-scale inputs. These findings highlight the significance of incorporating renormalon uncertainties in jet-related observables to provide an accurate understanding of hadronic processes.

Researchers study the frog model on trees of high degree and find that above a certain threshold, the probability of the model being in a transient state drops to near zero. This threshold marks the beginning of the model's recurrent phase. In trees of very high degree, this threshold is roughly half that value. It's also discovered that this threshold serves as a boundary for which the model's stationary distribution has non-zero support. This support may be seen as influencing the model's behavior during the recurrent phase. A new technique for analyzing the model is developed, which provides a precise expression for the model's stationary distribution in the recurrent phase. This expression reveals that the model's behavior is controlled by a self-adjoint operator that is a composition of the standard Wiener measure and a linear operator. This discovery may be of interest to researchers studying other systems that can be represented by similar compositions of measures and linear operators.

Research into magnetophotonic crystals with a surface plasmon resonance has focused on integrating multiple optical phenomena to achieve unique spectral characteristics. Our study reveals that the interaction between surface plasmons and Rayleigh anomalies in photonic crystals contributes significantly to the formation of the stop band, and this interaction causes the plasmon's effective localization to shift. Additionally, near the point of integration between the two, further complex spectral features emerge as a result of interference. This phenomenon leads to the appearance of an additional, broader stop band when viewing the spectrum from a broader perspective, and consists of several resonant peaks that arise from the interaction between the surface plasmon and the Rayleigh anomaly. This broader stop band can provide a foundation for the development of ultra-fast magnetophotonic devices. A hypothetical material with a 0.5 eV energy gap is examined computationally, and the predicted outcomes are verified through experimental measurements of the transmission characteristics of a magnetophotonic crystal, revealing the existence of the broader stop band and the complex spectral features in our model. The existence of these additional spectral features makes possible the development of ultra-fast magnetophotonic devices, and this includes the capability to build a fast magnetophotonic switch.

A recent knowledge distillation approach called DB3 is gaining attention for its effectiveness in compressing large neural networks using just a simple model. Despite its promise, DB3 remains poorly understood, and most current research involves treating it as a black box. In an effort to shed light on DB3's inner workings, this study endeavors to dissect its inner mechanisms and contrast them with established knowledge distillation methods. Our analysis reveals that DB3's ability to achieve comparable performance using fewer parameters is primarily a result of reducing noise in the data rather than obtaining more accurate model predictions. Additionally, our results demonstrate that DB3's performance can be further enhanced by utilizing a stronger teacher model and applying self-distillation. However, our analysis also uncovers a critical drawback of DB3, which involves a propensity for models to become overly confident. In order to address this issue, we propose a straightforward technique for regulating the confidence of neural networks. Our findings are backed by a comprehensive set of experiments conducted across diverse network architectures and datasets.

Determining the ratios of branching fractions for specific decay paths, such as $\Lambda_b^0 \to p J/ψγ$ over $\Lambda_b^0 \to p J/ψ$, involves analyzing $\Lambda_b^0$ decays obtained from $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV using LHCb data. These ratios have been calculated with certain uncertainties including those related to particle flux, recording efficiency, and particle count, all at 94% confidence. Based on an integrated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-2}$, the ratio of branching fractions was found to be $[1.06 \pm 0.17 \pm 0.10]\times 10^{-4}$ for $\Lambda_b^0 \to p J/ψγ$ over $\Lambda_b^0 \to p J/ψ$. Furthermore, the calculation yielded a fraction of direct $B^0 \to J/ψγ$ decays at $(5.3 \pm 0.8 \pm 0.4) \times 10^{-4}$.

Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a semisimple Lie algebra and $V$ a multiplicity-free $\mathfrak{g}$-module. The main theorem of this study establishes that if the composition factor map from the module $V$ to its submodule lattice is surjective, then this condition holds for all submodules of $V$. The proof relies on the fundamental theorem of finite semigroups and groups to derive desired conclusions about the submodules of $V$, demonstrating that composition factor map from $V$ to its submodule lattice is an epimorphism. This result can be applied to simplify the proof of a prior finding by Kempkes and van der Giessen, regarding module $V$ with a specific composition factor map property. The theorem in question holds either (1) the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{a}_{2n}$ for $n \geq 2$ and modules $V$ with highest weight being multiple weights of the form $2\omega_i + \omega_j$, or (2) the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{a}_{2n+1}$ for $n \geq 2$ and modules $V$ with highest weight being multiple weights of the form $\omega_i + 2\omega_j$.

The concept of geodetic sets was initially introduced by the authors of $[1]$, who then proposed the strong geodetic recognition problem and a related decision problem, aiming to investigate the effectiveness of using linear time algorithms to solve these problems, particularly on sparse graphs. Specifically, given a subset of vertices $X$ in a graph $G$, determine if $X$ is a strong geodetic subset of $G$ in linear time. This paper establishes a key result, proving that this task can be accomplished in linear time $O(|X|+|E|)$ by identifying and sorting the geodetic neighborhoods of the vertices in $X$. Building upon this result, the paper also shows that determining if a vertex set $X$ contains a strong geodetic subset is NP-complete, even when considering graphs with no cycles and $X$ consisting of two vertices.

When teaching an unskilled robot to mimic a skilled colleague, the process is complicated by two issues: finding the optimal policy efficiently and gathering a sufficient amount of diverse expert data. To tackle these challenges, we've developed a trail-blazing efficient policy learning strategy, which involves two key components: a trail-following algorithm that significantly reduces the necessary computations and leverages weak supervision, and a trail-design method that generates a limited yet representative set of expert examples through a carefully structured reward engineering approach. By integrating these methods, we've created an efficient trail-based imitation learning system that outperforms existing benchmarks by up to 300% in terms of sample efficiency in various robotic tasks and settings. Additionally, our trial-based approach succeeds in reducing the required expert demonstrations by half while maintaining policy performance.

We introduce Co-Imitation Learning, a groundbreaking new approach that allows multiple non-expert agents to learn from one another and an elite model of an intricate game. Co-IL enables these co-learners to acquire a comparable level of performance to the elite model by leveraging the shared knowledge that underpins the game. In our experiments, we find that Co-IL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods, even in complex multi-agent scenarios. Our findings demonstrate that Co-IL can achieve a level of performance comparable to that of an elite model with a significantly reduced dataset, requiring as little as one-fiftieth of the data typically needed. This breakthrough leads us to propose Co-IL as a more efficacious alternative to imitation learning, which often relies heavily on expensive and time-consuming data collection of expert demonstrations. Our code and data are available for download at https://github.com/Nethbah/Co-Imitation-Learning.

The issue of a sequential decoder making errors due to an incorrect polarized cutoff rate was explored in our previous research, specifically when the rate exceeds the highest entropy value among the source components. In this research, we aim to examine the impact of selecting the polarized cutoff rate as a bias value on the decoder's error probability. We establish and prove an upper limit for the modified error probability distribution $p_{Y^{n}}\left(\left\{0,1\right\}^{n}\right)$, where this limit results in a simpler expression that directly relates to the difference between the chosen bias, highest entropy component, and the logarithm of the sequence's base two length. We utilize this new understanding to derive a stricter upper limit for the error probability $p_{Y^{n}}\left(\left\{0,1\right\}^{n}\right)$, where this limit is proportional to the sequence's length $2^{nR_{0}}$, specifically when the chosen bias equals the highest entropy component among the source components. Moreover, we find that the sequence's binary structure allows it to achieve the proposed upper limit, providing us with a specific example and result in the case where the sequence's base two length is a power of two.

Previous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of reinforcement learning in improving translation quality. Nonetheless, the underlying issue with conventional approaches lies in the excessive dimensionality of their action spaces. This research proposes a novel technique to reduce the action space dimensionality while maintaining its expressive capacity. We introduce an innovative way to generate a compact action space and incorporate a precision-enhancing method for the resulting simplified space. Consequently, this is met with significant performance gains in our experiments covering WMT English-to-German and Czech-to-English translation tasks, yielding better results than prior works and establishing new benchmarks.

Deep learning-based methods are gaining popularity for calibrating robots due to their ability to establish relationships between camera views and end-effector poses. Introducing an efficient approach to enhance end-effector pose estimation using a single camera and deep learning, our methodology incorporates a specially designed network that leverages a depth camera's readings to improve robustness in calibration processes. Unlike conventional two-stage approaches, our unified framework achieves optimal performance with a single-stage, 2D-to-3D alignment architecture, outperforming existing methods according to precision metrics on the newly created EndEffectorPose Dataset (EEP). Our technique proves valuable for tasks like docking and grasping, and we provide code and dataset access at https://github.com/frostisz/EEPNet.

This study explores the relationship between continuous retracts and Quasi-Finitely Generated Spaces (QFS-spaces). It begins by examining the retracts of QFS-spaces and shows they have equivalent properties to the space itself. It then establishes that the intersection of any family of QFS-spaces is itself a QFS-space, and this result leads to a broader conclusion about the retracts of these spaces. Finally, the study demonstrates that the concept of continuous retracts can be applied to expand our understanding of QFS-spaces.

The rise of personalization on the Web has led many to speculate that users' browsing habits are no longer a random stroll across the internet, but rather a reflection of their own biases. This notion has significant implications for our understanding of online influence and political polarization. In this research, we take a different approach, separating users' browsing habits from the underlying website structure to investigate their individual effects on polarization. Our analysis of a comprehensive dataset of hyperlinks on the Web reveals that, even when structural connections are factored out, users' browsing habits contribute significantly to polarization. In contrast, website structures have a minimal impact on polarization. Additionally, our analysis shows that users' browsing habits differ substantially from the underlying website structures, with nearly half of visited pages having no connection to the previous page. These findings suggest that online influence operates through a complex, layered mechanism in which both website structures and user browsing habits play distinct roles. As a result, we propose a new model that combines these layers to provide a theoretical foundation for future online influence studies.

We make the groundbreaking observation that the word problem for Thompson's group V corresponds to determining whether a deterministic context-free string can be reduced to a notably simple context-free target string. This connection arises from a novel, underlying recognition of V's action as a deterministic context-free rewriting process. Building upon this understanding, we develop an essential insight connecting the group's action to the recognition of right-loop-free context-free languages, a significant expansion of its theoretical applications.

Quantum non-equilibrium systems can't maintain an unidirectional information exchange with their surroundings, as opposed to classical systems. A necessary condition for an open quantum system to exchange information bidirectionally is that it must be in a non-overlapping state in the context of scattering states. Utilizing quantum network concepts, we demonstrate that this requirement can be relaxed when working with multi-partite states by showcasing an example involving three lasers connected to an optical cavity. The cavity can exchange bidirectional information with the lights, regardless of whether the lights are overlapping or not, thereby allowing for the effective control of the cavity's state.

This research paper addresses two primary objectives. First, it examines how recurrent operators affect the condition for biharmonic hypersurfaces to be minimal within the Euclidean space. Secondly, it identifies both the type and the proper interval where both the biharmonic and recurrent operators conditions hold true.

We define a generalisation of the set of fractions with denominator powers of a prime number and investigate its subsets that can be recognised by infinite automata using p/q-regular expressions. Our analysis focuses on the characterisation of these subsets in the context of d-dimensional space. By extending a previously known property, we find that a subset of the set (N_p/q)^d is p/q-recognisable if and only if its elements can be reordered such that for any three consecutive fractions with the same denominator, the product of the middle two fractions is less than 1. This condition enables us to establish a connection between the order of fractions in (N_p/q)^d and their corresponding order in R^d. As a result, we are able to prove that our definition of p/q-recognisability is equivalent to using real-valued automata in a specific topological space. Additionally, we explore the concept of p/q-regularity in the context of single-dimensional space and identify the sets (N_p/q)* and R_p/q as being p/q-regular.

A complex, comprehensive model of particle physics has been developed, based on the principles of supersymmetry and the concept of modular symmetry. This $a_u$MSM model effectively resolves three major issues facing the standard model of particle physics: the presence of too many free parameters, the absence of a clear explanation for the strong CP problem, and the instability of the electroweak vacuum. By incorporating six extra families of fermions and 21 additional gauge bosons, the $a_u$MSM model achieves these goals through its modular symmetry framework, which in turn generates an acceptable magnitude for the neutrino MSW splitting. Furthermore, the $a_u$MSM model predicts that the number of quark flavors is linked to a power of the modular weight, which results in a specific relationship between the masses of the different quark families. This theory is compatible with existing experimental data and predicts outcomes for various processes that can be verified through upcoming experiments.

Our research is centered on the LAMOST time-domain survey, which has generated a comprehensive catalog of 107,107 binary candidates spanning 13.5 years across 12,186 unique objects. This catalog was created by combining data from six surveys and incorporates information from optical light curves, radial velocity curves, and stellar Stroumger indices. With a diverse range of 4.4 magnitudes in k_e (3.0-7.4), this catalog comprises 46,779 long-period binary candidates, 27,109 solar-constrained period binary candidates, and 33,219 short-period binary candidates. Notably, this is the largest collection of binary candidates identified to date. Our analysis reveals a binary density of 0.60±0.01 per square parsec, consistent with previous findings. The distribution of mass ratios in this catalog follows a 2.5 power law, identical to that observed in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey binary catalog. Additionally, our research includes a novel approach to estimating the detection efficiency of binary candidates based on their characteristics. This efficiency model indicates that approximately 78% of binaries in the sample were detected, with an equal chance for long-period and solar-constrained period binaries. Our study may be used as a foundation for future analyses aimed at understanding the binary population in our galaxy.

In the context of image segmentation, a significant challenge lies in modeling complex interactions within the scene for an End-to-End learning approach. To address this, we introduce Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), a novel architecture that incorporates non-overlapping sub-networks to complement each other by injecting external information at every convolutional layer. Our proposed EG-CNNs simply adds an edge-gating mechanism to Convolutional Neural Networks, where the primary contribution involves exploiting cross-path interactions to synthesize diverse feature maps. This leads to improved performance in semantic segmentation tasks, as our method easily integrates with common backbone networks. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed EG-CNNs outperform baseline methods, such as UNet and U-Net variants, by a significant margin on the Cityscapes dataset. Additionally, our method showcases comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches, such as DeepLabv3+, while possessing the benefit of reduced parameters.

We examine current implementations of distributed databases with advanced concurrency control, such as MongoDB, Postgres, and Couchbase, and find that their underlying storage engines lack a formal analysis of their concurrency properties. To address this gap, we introduce a theoretical framework based on formal methods to specify, verify, and validate the concurrency behaviors of distributed database storage engines. Applying our framework to three real-world deployments – WIREDTIGER in MongoDB, REPLICASET in MongoDB, SHARDEDCLUSTER in MongoDB, and COUCH in Couchbase – we find that their concurrency behaviors do not match their claimed properties and may lead to invalid states and lost updates. To rectify this issue, we propose modifications to these deployments and prove that our suggested changes yield snapshot isolation, robust to concurrent transactions and data fragmentation. Moreover, our results provide implicit verification of concurrency control in these deployments, obviating the need for explicit checking. To facilitate further research, we outline a method for generating transaction triggers that ensures verifiable concurrency behaviors. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we present a prototype implementation, incorporating our theoretical framework, to formally specify, verify, and validate the concurrency behaviors of these distributed database storage engines. This work lays the ground for a methodical approach to designing reliable distributed database storage engines.

Given a Dyck path $\pi$, the concept of $e$-positivity for chromatic symmetric functions $E(\pi)$ holds true if its expression as a sum of monomials, with coefficients $e^n$, is nonnegative for all $n$. A key aspect of this property is understanding which chromatic symmetric functions in the family $E(\pi)$ remain nonnegative. Our research focuses on determining whether $E(\pi)$ meets the $e$-positivity criterion for a specific, carefully defined subset of Dyck paths $\pi$. To approach this challenge, we develop a key insight by establishing a link between $e$-positivity and another property known as $h$-vector positivity. To apply this connection, we need to examine $h$-vector positivity for a broader spectrum of Dyck paths. As a result of our analysis, we uncover new instances of $h$-vector positivity, thereby contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of this property. Furthermore, our findings enable us to conclude that $E(\pi)$ is nonnegative for all alternating permutations $\pi$, thereby extending a prior finding to a broader class of objects.

The idea of hindsight summarization can be used to reduce the impact of prediction errors by selectively removing past predictions based on new information. This concept has the potential to enhance machine learning methods by limiting the influence of prior errors. We explore how a summarization function can be optimized to minimize the effect of prediction mistakes in sequential tasks, demonstrating that an optimal summarization approach yields substantial improvements in prediction accuracy in both simple linear and complex neural network models. We also examine two practical summarization techniques: one focuses on correcting previous predictions by comparing them to the actual outcomes, and another involves identifying the relationships between previous predictions and new data. These methods are applicable across various evaluation metrics, including mean squared error and accuracy. We provide mathematical proofs to verify the benefits of hindsight summarization and illustrate its performance with theoretical and numerical analyses. Our results show that hindsight summarization can lead to significant reductions in prediction errors in sequences of data.

The success of machine learning models in medical image analysis depends on their ability to perform well in various clinical settings. However, research has shown that these models can suffer from a decrease in performance when exposed to different patient demographics, indicating a significant challenge to create universally applicable images. A crucial factor contributing to this limitation is the presence of implicit biases within medical imaging datasets, which can impede the development of future models. In this study, we investigate the presence of implicit biases in six publicly accessible datasets utilized for automatic detection systems, comprising three datasets for chest computed tomography and CT angiography and three for brain magnetic resonance imaging. Our analysis reveals the presence of demographic preferences in raw data but finds that they can be effectively eliminated through data augmentation techniques without compromising the quality of the dataset. Moreover, our results demonstrate that removing implicit biases does not hinder the performance of detection networks, as they are capable of generalizing to demographic groups both within and outside the training dataset. Our research comprises six diverse datasets, incorporating multiple imaging modalities and organs, thereby providing a comprehensive foundation for the investigation of implicit biases in medical imaging and paving the way for future research in this domain.

We examine how the shape of hysteresis loops evolves in an isolated cluster of three connected Ising spins, where the interaction between any two spins is either extremely weak or extremely strong, similar to a binary compound known as Bismuth Strontium Calcium Lead Oxide. Utilizing a temperature-ferromagnetic field phase diagram, we find that varying the strength of interactions between any two spins can significantly alter the loop's shape, moving from a semi-circle in strong interaction cases to exhibit asymmetry when the interaction is weak, particularly when heated above the surrounding magnetic transition temperature.

New measurements taken by the Parker Solar Probe provide the most precise data on the energy required to escape the solar gravitational pull at very short heliocentric distances. Compared to existing observations at 1 AU, the new data feature significantly higher injection energies, which exceed 2.5 times the median value when collected near 37 million kilometers from the sun, and exhibit a much broader distribution in this proximity. In this study, the energy distributions from the Parker Solar Probe and other sources are analyzed in relation to solar wind speed, finding a notable correlation between these factors near the sun, particularly in this proximity, where fast wind escape energies compared to slow wind speeds widen to more than 5 times the median value, showing a significant relationship that deepens as you move closer to the sun. In this proximity, the energy distributions also differentiate between streams and displays corotational flow patterns, where streams exhibit broader variations and show a notable spike at the solar wind's escape energy in this proximity, suggesting an interaction between the solar wind and the solar magnetic field, where any breach of continuity may indicate a connection to the solar plasma heating issue.

Multilingual emotion recognition has seen significant advancements in recent years. However, the complexity of understanding emotions differs significantly between languages and requires a more sophisticated approach than just translating words into standard English words. To address this challenge, the paper proposes a novel framework called the Bilingual Integrated Contextualized Affective Dictionary (BICAD). This model is a dual-system approach that combines two components: a pre-trained multilingual contextualized affective dictionary and a BICAD update system. To achieve consistency across languages and minimize bias, the paper introduces two methods: correlated dictionary learning and biased data rejection. By incorporating a degree of freedom for each word to deviate from a one-to-one language mapping, the model shows significant improvements in recognizing emotions on four diverse datasets translated from English to German, French, and Chinese. The proposed BICAD model demonstrates an impressive 23% better performance than current standards and highlights the importance of considering the differences between language mappings in emotion recognition.

Applying high hydrostatic pressure causes a significant transformation in the lattice parameters of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$, a complex oxide with spirally interconnected rods, leading to a structural phase transition from the $a$-axis preferred tetragonal phase to a $c$-axis preferred phase, preferring the $a$2$'$-axis under high pressure. The transition is accompanied by the initiation of a $2c$ supercell and the polarization of Bi$^{3+}$ ions across the structure, leading to an increase in the $c$/$a$ ratio from around 2.5 to over 3, along with the direct engagement of Ti$^{4+}$ ions in the octahedral framework, for a pressure of around 8 GPa. The material exhibits an unexpected and notable shift in its optical characteristics, with an increase in the bandgap energy from about 2.3 to 3.2 eV, along with a shift in its optical absorption towards the ultraviolet region, and the material displays an impressive dielectric constant of over 1000, even at high pressures. The study provides a theoretical understanding of these phenomena with the use of calculations based on structural data obtained under high pressure, revealing that the bandgap increase results from a rise in the covalency of chemical bonds and a shift in the electronic population from the $a$-axis to the $c$-axis, leading to a

We analyze the impact of an error bound comparison on the Euler scheme for stochastic differential equations with rough boundaries, demonstrating that a localized error bound comparison results in reduced accurate discrete paths, specifically O(dt^(1/2)) instead of the usual dt accurate paths, and further depends on the comparison function's smoothness. This finding motivates the introduction of a higher-order strong scheme with an expanded error bound comparison, enabling larger feasible time steps while maintaining comparable levels of accuracy, albeit with increased computational cost. A specific second-order scheme is proposed and its error bound established, illustrating its potential for improving solution efficiency.

The problem of weak shock waves in fluids with arbitrary adiabatic powers was long thought to be similar to the problem of steady, one-dimensional long waves. However, it has been proven that for shock waves with extremely high adiabatic powers, there is a unique, abrupt change in the fluid's behavior near the shock's center. This region is characterized by a specific power that depends solely on the shock's relative strength and where the fluid's velocity suddenly drops to near zero. This discovery challenges the idea that there is a direct relationship between the fluid's velocity and distance from the shock's center and instead indicates that the velocity exhibits a singular, oscillatory pattern due to an infinite number of harmonic oscillations existing within the shock wave. This result was initially demonstrated by Rayleigh in 1913 for shocks with infinite adiabatic powers and has since been expanded to include a broader range of powers. This expansion shows that the oscillations, despite being composed of an infinite number of waves, retain a distinct frequency and amplitude and resonate with the fluid's velocity to create the appearance of a singular, oscillating point at the shock's center. This phenomenon was first observed in the 19th century by Mach and Emile in their study of the flow of gases over obstacles and was later numerically modeled by Karlson and Shmarev using the method of matched asymptotic expansions. This understanding of the behavior of strong shock waves has significant implications for our knowledge of these waves and may provide

We examine the instanton-calculated decay rates for heavy-quark decays, specifically within the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert and Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed parametrization schemes, and systematically compare their decay patterns to establish a unifying framework. This comparative analysis reveals the inherent relationships between various parameters in both schemes, ultimately allowing us to derive the Instanton-Sum Rules which connect physical parameters to their fundamental counterparts. These rules demonstrate the intricate connections between physical parameters, decay patterns, and calculable instanton effects in QCD.

We derive a new one-dimensional supersymmetric potential that remains non-singular, making a significant contribution to the development of theories beyond the harmonic oscillator potential. The new potential is demonstrated to be a variation of the deformed harmonic oscillator and the diatomic oscillator, both of which belong to the DEFORMED POLYNOMIAL HEISENBERG ALGEBRA (DPPHA) class. DPPHA serves as the fundamental framework for our analysis, utilizing the Schrödinger picture and providing a clear, detailed explanation of the potential's formation.

This subject introduces key ideas in the dynamics of natural systems, beginning with a review of stability principles and the concept of lyapunov exponents, which demonstrates the fundamental connection between local expansion or contraction and system behavior near equilibrium or periodic orbits.

Researchers studied an asymmetric Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) consisting of two Josephson junctions to understand how they switch current compared to a single junction. The presence of phase locking between the junctions was investigated, and the effect analyzed for both symmetric and asymmetric loops. The study shows that in an asymmetric loop, the switching current can be higher or lower than in an isolated junction, depending on the loop's symmetry, and that this difference can be significant due to phase locking. The theoretical framework developed here can be applied to control the switching current in an asymmetric SQUID, essential for the coherent oscillations of a superconducting quantum bit located at the SQUID's center.

We've analyzed the non-abelian aether theory within a thermodynamic framework, particularly focusing on how temperature influences the interaction between two parallel plates in a vacuum. This investigation considered both constant temperature and pressure to derive the non-abelian Casimir force, and revealed that temperature affects the force in an exponential manner. We found that temperature increases the non-abelian Casimir force in comparison to the zero-temperature limit, and that this impact is more pronounced at higher temperatures. Interestingly, temperature does not alter the $T^{4}$ dependence of the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law, despite appearing in the effective action as a dynamical field. The result also indicates that the non-abelian aether term contributes to the non-abelian Casimir energy, which in turn affects the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law by increasing the reflection coefficients that control the energy transmission between the plates.

This research develops a speed and cost model that accounts for the expected liquidity costs of a delta-hedging strategy, quantifying the anticipated slippage before hedging. We devise an efficient computational method to determine these expected costs, employing a combination of the Black-Scholes formula and Monte Carlo simulation. This technique allows us to calculate expected liquidity costs quickly, which can be done much faster than utilizing straight Monte Carlo simulation. We further examine the performance of this method against the more conventional approach of calculating expected costs through the simulation of specific hedging scenarios.

This research extends the scope of variational principles for integral functionals at work in linearly constrained settings, common in the study of heterogeneous materials, to also consider non-yield conditions and singular potentials. Building on a comprehensive framework, the analysis focuses on boundary conditions, defining the functional's minimizers within specified domains, and then delves into the significance of its compact support. Key approaches employed include the integration of relaxation and linearization methods, with additional insights gained through the use of scalar auxiliary functions. The findings offer a detailed understanding of the variational principles' behavior and relevance to the study of heterogeneous materials exhibiting complex, nonlinear, and discontinuous patterns.

We've analyzed high-resolution Hubble Space Telescope images to investigate tidal features in 103 early-type galaxies. Our study shows a notable correlation between tidal features and the galaxies' mass: a significant proportion of tidal features are found in more massive galaxies. Furthermore, within a given mass range, more massive galaxies exhibit a greater mass-to-light ratio, contributing to a higher tidal feature fraction. Our analysis suggests tidal features contribute around 5-15% of the total galaxy mass. A separate analysis reveals a significant correlation between tidal features and giant elliptical galaxies at the centers of clusters, specifically within the Coma cluster. It's observed that around 24% of these galaxies feature a tidal counterpart, compared to a 9% rate in more isolated clusters. Many of these tidal features exhibit distinct stellar populations, indicating they have an estimated age range of around 1-3 billion years. Many early-type galaxies in the Coma cluster also display a notable increase in their tidal feature fractions above 1.5 times the solar mass, suggesting a possible influence of cluster environments on their galaxy-scale mass assemblies.

A key concept in the study of social mobility is that of opportunities, which refers to the resources and chances available to individuals that can aid them in overcoming adversity and achieving a higher socioeconomic status. The issue of intergenerational mobility is complex because it involves both the effects of past circumstances on present conditions and the influence of current circumstances on future prospects. This paper presents a mathematical model that incorporates the concept of opportunities and investigates how they are allocated across different socioeconomic groups. The model reveals that the distribution of opportunities is a crucial driver of mobility, especially in regards to how it affects the chances of mobility for individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. However, the model also shows that the relationship between opportunities and mobility can be non-linear and even counter-intuitive in certain situations. This is particularly evident when there are significant disparities in wealth and health across different groups, as seen in the case of the United States during the period of 1979 to 2016. The findings of this study provide new insights into the dynamics of mobility and highlight the need for more comprehensive policies that aim to improve mobility. These policies should go beyond simply providing opportunities and also address issues of inequality and distribution, as well as consider the non-linear effects of opportunity on mobility.

Laser systems based on CPA and NLO, which utilize nonlinear optical processes to achieve high power and ultra-high peak power, are considered crucial for future high-power laser applications. However, accurately modeling these complex systems proves difficult due to the interaction between the nonlinear process and the CPA pulse, leading to an inherent link between the pulse duration and the system's saturation characteristics. In this paper, a novel approach to modeling these laser systems is introduced, separating the nonlinear process from the CPA pulse and instead modeling the pulse duration as a function of the system's saturation characteristics. This approach is shown to significantly simplify the modeling process, enabling easy calculation of the pulse duration and spectral characteristics for any given system parameters. In addition, this approach can be applied to various nonlinear optical processes, including second-harmonic generation, sum-frequency generation, Raman amplifiers, and supercontinuum generation. Examples illustrating the proposed method's effectiveness and advantages can be found in the accompanying paper.

For $p = 2$, it is known that the linear operators on $\ell_2^n$ have a dense subset which achieves any desired isometry on the unit ball.
